# pathland-server-core — implementation status

**Last updated:** September 12, 2026

The transport-agnostic Pathland server runtime: one app instance per session (SSR +
live 16-byte opcode deltas + environment) and the session registry, shared by the Spring
Boot and Quarkus starters. No web-framework dependency — framework glue lives in the
starters.

## Implemented

- **`PathlandApp`** — the app's root-view factory (`View newRoot()` + optional
  `theme()`); the single app-specific piece a starter needs.
- **`PathlandConnection`** — the transport seam (`send(byte[])`/`isOpen()`); each starter
  adapts its WebSocket type to it.
- **`PathlandSession`** — per-session: builds the `Platform.ACTIVE_PATH` signal, mounts
  `app.newRoot().environment(ACTIVE_PATH, activePath)`, send-on-`endFrame` sink over a
  `PathlandConnection`, `applyEnvironment` (re-route guard-aware via the bound router),
  `dispatch` (tap/nav-intent/text/value/date/NAVIGATE), `resync`, `renderHtml`, `close`.
- **`PathlandRegistry`** — session lifecycle: single actor thread, 1:1 sessions keyed by
  id, lazy creation on first environment message, pending connections,
  `open`/`environment`/`dispatch`/`resync`/`close`/`renderHtml`/`shutdown`.
- **`StateStores`** — default state store: Redis when reachable, else the supplied
  fallback.

## Not implemented / gaps

- No multi-node/shared sessions (each server owns its sessions in-memory).

## Verified by

`mvn test` — `PathlandSessionTest`: mounts + routes taps through the binding maps,
`applyEnvironment`/`resync`/`close` idempotent, registry SSR + lifecycle/teardown.

Spring Boot auto-configuration for Pathland: SSR at any path, live deltas over `/ws`,

## Implemented

- **`SpringConnection`** — adapts `WebSocketSession` to `PathlandConnection`.

@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApp {

    @Bean PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
}

activates the registry and SSR renders the root. Manual: the `pathland-spring-boot-demo`

# pathland-quarkus-starter — implementation status

**Last updated:** September 12, 2026

Quarkus integration for Pathland: SSR at any path, live deltas over `/ws`, per-session
state. Adding the starter dependency + a `PathlandApp` CDI bean gives a running app.

## Implemented

- **`IndexResource`** — JAX-RS SSR catch-all (`/` + deep links, `/ws` excluded via
  negative lookahead) + `session` cookie.
- **`PathlandRegistryProducer`** — CDI `@Produces @Singleton` `PathlandRegistry` from the
  app's `PathlandApp` bean + default store (Redis-or-in-memory); `@Disposes` shuts it down.
- **`QuarkusConnection`** — adapts `WebSocketConnection` to `PathlandConnection`.
- `META-INF/beans.xml` so Quarkus discovers the starter.

@ApplicationScoped
public class MyApp implements PathlandApp {
    public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); }
}

fallback; a WebSocket handshake to `/ws` returns 101. Core behavior is covered by

=== README ===
# Pathland Protocol

> A cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol for declarative, retained-mode UI
>
> **Status: proof of concept.** Not production software — the wire format and APIs may change before 1.0.

[![CI](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

## Overview

Pathland is a **protocol-first** UI framework for **retained-mode UI** with
multiple renderer backends. It offers a declarative, retained-mode view API
(SwiftUI-shaped in ergonomics) designed to be **language-agnostic** and
**platform-agnostic**.

As of August 2026 the core is a **Rust opcode engine**. It emits the
application's **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
padding, alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer** into shared
linear memory. Each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that
platform's **native elements** (GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the
browser, HTML server-side) and those native elements lay themselves out.

On desktop the engine runs **natively**: other languages drive it through the
flat **native C ABI** (`pathland-view-native`) over a zero-copy shared ring and render
through the shared GTK renderer (`pathland-render-gtk`).

The **16-byte opcode engine is transport- and process-agnostic by design**. The
ring buffer is a plain region of shared linear memory, so the engine runs
wherever the producer and consumer can exchange bytes — no assumptions about
where the application lives. The same engine spans **embedded systems**
(FreeRTOS dual-core queues passing opcode slices between cores), **pure
in-browser client-side apps** (a WASM Web Worker producing into a
`SharedArrayBuffer` that the main-thread DOM renderer consumes), and
**server-driven enterprise architectures** (Java/C# backends emitting opcode
frames over WebSocket or gRPC). Transport and process boundaries are details of
delivery, never of the protocol.

**The engine does not compute layout and does not emit rects.** It describes
*what* the UI is, never *where* it is. Emission is **diff-based and reactive**:
change detection is fine-grained and signal-based — a signal bound to a node's
text or a property re-emits only that node's deltas, so only the things that
actually changed emit opcodes and an unchanged tree emits zero opcodes.

## Enterprise positioning — replace the BFF + Rich Frontend paradigm

For server-driven web teams, Pathland is positioned as a replacement for the
**whole BFF + Rich Frontend stack** — and for libraries like **HTMX** that patch
around it. Today's enterprise stack pays for a JSON API tier (a BFF), a
client-side state model, a SPA framework, and a build pipeline, all to render UI
the server already owns. Pathland removes that layer: the backend **is** the
application. It declares the entire UI in its own language (Java, Rust, C#, …),
emits **binary deltas** over WebSocket, and the client is a thin hydration layer
that applies them and reports raw input back — no BFF contract to maintain, no
client state model, no SPA framework, no separate frontend team.

- **Server-driven, like HTMX — but a protocol, not a script tag.** The web
  client is a small vanilla-JS hydrator that decodes self-contained `PLPL`
  batches and applies opcode deltas in place; everything else lives in the
  backend, where enterprise teams can test, observe, and secure it.
- **Native elements everywhere.** The same opcode stream drives GTK4 widgets on
  desktop, DOM elements in the browser, and SSR HTML — one view definition, any
  renderer, any language.
- **Binary and diff-based.** Fixed 16-byte opcodes, zero emission for an
  unchanged tree, self-contained frames over the wire.
- **Enterprise-ready by design** (see Project Status): Java 17+ across the whole
  stack, a single Rust HTML renderer reused by every language, WebSocket
  resilience, metrics/health, security hardening, and WCAG 2.1 AA.

## Project Status

**Proof of concept.** Pathland is a working reference implementation for
validating the protocol, not production software. The 16-byte opcode engine,
the Rust and Java DSLs, the GTK4 / HTML renderers, and the
SSR + WebSocket demos are all functional (tests green), but the wire format
(version 1) and every API are subject to change before a 1.0.

## The Three Elements

Pathland is composed of three elements. They are the vocabulary the whole
project speaks, so they are settled and used consistently:

```
┌────────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────┐
│ 1. Retained UI     │   │ 2. Opcode engine   │   │ 3. Renderer         │
│ the app's UI tree  │──⇢│ reconciles + emits │──⇢│ maps opcodes onto   │
│ (any language,     │   │                    │   │ native elements +   │
│  any platform)     │   │                    │   │ event reporting     │
└────────────────────┘   └────────────────────┘   └─────────────────────┘
```

1. **Retained UI** — the application's canonical retained UI tree. It is the
   single source of truth, owned by the application. It can be authored in
   **any language on any platform**: Rust, Java, Swift, C#, C, TypeScript —
   desktop, mobile, or embedded — through a generated DSL or the flat native C
   ABI.
2. **Opcode engine** — the producer: reconciles the retained tree and emits it as
   fixed **16-byte opcodes** using fine-grained, signal-based change detection: a
   signal bound to a node's text or a property re-emits only that node's deltas,
   so only the things that actually changed emit and an unchanged tree emits zero
   opcodes. The engine is language-independent — the same opcode stream serves
   every renderer. It spans a pure protocol core (`pathland-core`) and a
   retained-tree emitter (`pathland-engine`).
3. **Renderer** — consumes the opcode stream and maps it onto that platform's
   **native elements**, and reports raw inputs back as events. It is a pure
   function of the opcode stream (stateless) and never retains application
   state. *"Host" and "driver" are roles a renderer plays: it runs inside a
   host and is pumped by a driver — they are not separate elements.* The same
   opcode stream targets **different UI systems**: a GTK4 renderer on desktop,
   an AppKit/SwiftUI renderer on macOS, a WinUI renderer on Windows, an LVGL
   renderer on embedded, a DOM renderer in the browser.

The opcodes are carried from the engine to the renderer by a transport (a
zero-copy shared-memory ring on desktop/native, a serialized network batch for
remote/browser); transport is an implementation detail, not a fourth element.

## Execution & Deployment Models

The fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer** is what makes Pathland
*process-agnostic*: the producer and consumer only need to share a region of
memory (or a byte stream), so the exact same engine and wire format serve five
distinct execution modes.

> **Implementation status:** the **native desktop** (c) and **distributed
> WebSocket** (d) paths — including the SSR HTML web client (the DOM renderer) — are
> implemented today. The **embedded** (a), **in-browser WASM** (b), and
> **microfrontend** (e) modes, the planned **gRPC** transport, and the
> SwiftUI/AppKit/WinUI renderers are **roadmap targets** enabled by the
> architecture (see the `*(planned)*` crates in the
> [Rust workspace](#rust-workspace)).

### a) Embedded Dual-Core (In-Process)

Core 0 runs application logic and sensor handling; Core 1 decodes opcodes and
renders **LVGL** over a **zero-copy SRAM ring buffer** (e.g. ESP32). The `no_std`
protocol core (`pathland-core`) emits into shared SRAM; the second core drains
the ring and drives LVGL widgets. No heap, no serialization — just a 16-byte
opcode stream across cores, passed through a FreeRTOS queue or a direct
SRAM producer/consumer pair.

### b) In-Browser Pure Client (Zero Main-Thread Lock)

Application logic runs in a **Web Worker compiled to WASM**. It emits opcodes
into a **`SharedArrayBuffer`** that the main thread's DOM renderer consumes
directly — bypassing Virtual DOM diffing entirely, because the renderer applies
only the delta opcodes to the native DOM. Since the worker never blocks the main
thread and the renderer is a pure function of the stream, this path targets
better sustained frame rates than single-threaded JS frameworks for large,
reactive trees.

### c) Native Desktop (IPC / Shared Memory)

Native apps drive the engine through the flat **C ABI** (`pathland-view-native`)
or **Java JNA** over a **zero-copy shared ring** into GTK4 / native widgets
(`pathland-render-gtk`). This is the current desktop path — producer and
renderer live in the same process and share the ring directly.

### d) Distributed Network (Server-Driven UI)

Backends (**Java Spring / Quarkus, C#**) emit self-contained opcode frames over
**WebSocket** (implemented) and, planned, **gRPC** directly to **Web (HTML)** or
mobile renderers. Frames are self-contained `PLPL`
batches, so each message is independent — no shared memory and no session state
in the renderer.

### e) Microfrontend Composition (Server-Side Merging)

The retained-tree model also opens the door to **true microfrontends without the
JavaScript-bundle hassle**: the subtrees of different services can be merged
into **one UI tree server-side** and relayed to the renderer as a single opcode
stream, so teams can ship UI with their own backend and any renderer receives a
unified UI — with no per-microservice client code.

## Core Principles

- **Protocol-first**: standardized, open protocol for UI components, events, and raw inputs
- **16-byte opcodes**: every instruction is a fixed 16 bytes — cache-line aligned, deterministic, linear decode
- **Declarative, not positioned**: the engine emits structure + constraint properties (spacing, padding, alignment); native renderers compute positions
- **Native elements everywhere**: GTK4 widgets, DOM elements, HTML — never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent
- **Reactive emission**: fine-grained, signal-based change detection — only the nodes that actually changed emit opcodes; steady state emits zero
- **Command-based**: UI updates are tree mutations (CREATE_NODE, DELETE_NODE, INSERT_CHILD, MOVE_CHILD, …), never serialized trees
- **Stateless renderers**: renderers are pure functions of the opcode stream; they retain only their own rendered output, never application state
- **Zero-copy**: ring and arena are plain regions of shared linear memory
- **Single-producer / single-consumer**: guest engine produces; host renderer consumes
- **Hand-written Java DSL**: the declarative view DSL lives as a reusable Java library (`com.pathland.view`), not generated code — one ergonomic surface for desktop, server (Spring/Quarkus), and embedded hosts

## Documentation

### Specification

- [Opcode Protocol](./spec/OPCODE.md) — **Primary specification** — fixed 16-byte opcodes, ring buffer, arena, reactive emission, design tokens
- [Primitive Views](./spec/PRIMITIVES.md) — the primitive views the protocol supports (declarative view groupings), with protocol component IDs and status
- [Core Modifiers](./spec/MODIFIERS.md) — the core modifiers (protocol `STYLE` properties), with property IDs and status
- [Core Events](./spec/EVENTS.md) — the core events (raw inputs), with event command IDs and listener bits
- [Conformance Test Vectors](./spec/CONFORMANCE.md) — golden byte arrays for validating implementations
- [DSL Authoring Contract](./spec/DSL.md) — the SwiftUI-shaped authoring surface (what an application developer writes); informative — the wire specs above are normative

## Rust Workspace

The implementation is under [`lib/rust/`](./lib/rust/):

| Crate | Element | Responsibility |
|-------|---------|----------------|
| `pathland-view` | Retained UI | Declarative view DSL: VStack/HStack/Text/Button + chainable modifiers building a `pathland-engine::Node` tree (`no_std`) |
| `pathland-core` | Opcode engine | Protocol core: fixed 16-byte opcode, ring buffer, bump arena, events, memory layout, Guest/Host/Frame surface (`no_std`, zero-alloc) |
| `pathland-engine` | Opcode engine | Emitter: retained tree types (`Node`/`Component`) + diff-based reactive emission + reactive **signals** (moved out of `pathland-core`) |
| `pathland-core-transport` | Opcode engine | Transport: shared-memory ring + network batch encode/decode + batching policy (`std`) |
| `pathland-render-gtk` | Renderer | GTK4 renderer (rlib + cdylib): opcode frames → native GTK widgets, incrementally |
| `pathland-render-html` | Renderer | HTML renderer: maps opcode frames onto declarative HTML (flex stacks, spans, buttons) as a pure function of the stream — the server-side/remote target |
| `pathland-view-native` | Retained UI projection | Native C-ABI shim + `NativeHost`: flat world over a zero-copy shared ring (Swift/Java/C#…) |
| `pathland-core-capi` | Opcode engine | Minimal shared-memory ring C ABI (`libpathland_core`): create/destroy, ring push, frame boundaries, arena alloc, zero-copy read, event drain/send |
| `pathland-render-gtk-demo` | Demo | Rust GTK4 demo: authors the DSL, renders through `pathland-render-gtk` (no GTK APIs) |
| `pathland-web-worker` *(planned)* | Opcode engine / Renderer | WASM logic Worker + `SharedArrayBuffer` DOM driver: application logic emits opcodes in a Web Worker; the main-thread DOM renderer consumes them zero-copy (in-browser pure-client mode) |
| `pathland-esp32` *(planned)* | Renderer | Dual-core HAL driver for microcontrollers: Core 0 → Core 1 opcode slices over an SRAM ring, mapped onto LVGL widgets (embedded dual-core mode) |

`pathland-web-worker` and `pathland-esp32` are roadmap targets; the existing
`no_std`/WASM-capable core (`pathland-core`) and the ring C ABI
(`pathland-core-capi`) are the building blocks they are planned on.

## Java Libraries

The reusable, framework-agnostic Java libraries live under [`lib/java/`](./lib/java/)
(Maven reactor, `org.pathland`, Java 17+ — every LTS from 17):

| Module | Package | Responsibility |
|--------|---------|----------------|
| `pathland-view` | `com.pathland.view` | Declarative view DSL (`View`, `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`, …), Angular-style signals/computed/effects (`com.pathland.view.signal`), fine-grained opcode emitter (`com.pathland.view.emit`), wire codec (`com.pathland.view.transport`), lazy JNA ring interop (`com.pathland.view.ffm`), cross-platform state (`com.pathland.view.state`: `StateStore`/`PersistentState`/`State`) |
| `pathland-view-processor` | `com.pathland.processor` | JSR 269 annotation processor: generates `<View>_StateBinder` for `State` fields (auto-keyed by field name) |
| `pathland-render-html` | `com.pathland.render.html` | Pure-function HTML renderer over the opcode stream (SSR) with `data-pathland-id` hydration |
| `pathland-state-redis` | `com.pathland.state.redis` | Redis-backed `StateStore` over Lettuce (Spring/Quarkus/desktop) |
| `pathland-demo-views` | `com.pathland.demo` | Shared kitchensink demo views (`KitchenSinkView` + per-section components) declaring `State` fields |
| `pathland-quarkus-demo` | `com.pathland.quarkus` | Quarkus SSR + WebSocket demo consuming the libraries |
| `pathland-spring-boot-demo` | `com.pathland.spring` | Spring Boot SSR + WebSocket demo consuming the same libraries |

The same `com.pathland.view` DSL (and `State` fields) runs unchanged on a Spring Boot
app, a Quarkus app, or a desktop app; a desktop host pushes opcodes into the Rust ring via
JNA (`pathland_ring_buffer_push`), while a server emits self-contained frames over WebSocket.

### Build & run the Java libraries

```bash
# Rust ring C ABI (only needed for the desktop JNA path)
cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi

# Build + test the whole Java reactor (runs on every LTS from Java 17)
export JAVA_HOME=<jdk-home-17-or-later>
cd lib/java && mvn -q install

# Run the Quarkus SSR + WebSocket demo in dev mode (hot reload)
cd lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo && mvn quarkus:dev      # http://localhost:8080

# ...or run the packaged runner
cd lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo
mvn -q package
java -jar target/quarkus-app/quarkus-run.jar   # http://localhost:8080

# Run the Spring Boot SSR + WebSocket demo (same shared views)
cd lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-demo
mvn -q package
java -jar target/pathland-spring-boot-demo-0.1.0.jar   # http://localhost:8080
```

The libraries run on **every LTS from Java 17** (the environment is thread-local and
native interop is JNA, so nothing needs a preview/25-only JDK), with
**Quarkus ≥ 3.18** and **Spring Boot ≥ 3.5**.

### Run tests

```bash
cd lib/rust && cargo test
cd lib/java && mvn test

# no_std / wasm32 direction guard (requires: rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown)
cd lib/rust && ./check-wasm.sh
```

### Run the GTK desktop demo (native, zero-copy shared ring)

```bash
cd lib/rust && PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" cargo run -p pathland-render-gtk-demo
```

## Web Client (the DOM renderer — `lib/typescript`)

The browser client is the **SSR HTML renderer** (`pathland-render-html`, and its
Java counterpart `com.pathland.render.html`), hydrated by the **Pathland DOM
renderer** — `@pathland/dom-renderer` (TypeScript, `lib/typescript/`, no runtime
deps). Built as `dist/pathland-dom-renderer.js` and copied into both demos'
static resources, it hydrates the server-rendered DOM by `data-pathland-id`,
decodes each self-contained `PLPL` batch (bounds-checked), applies `STYLE`
deltas **and `TREE` structural deltas** in place, and sends raw-input events
back over the `/ws` socket. Styling is server-owned (Tailwind classes in the
SSR HTML); runtime style deltas are applied by the DOM renderer as inline style
and design tokens as CSS variables.

## Components & Properties

Component and property IDs are defined in `pathland-core`'s
[`constants.rs`](./lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs),
documented in [OPCODE.md](./spec/OPCODE.md), and catalogued by category in
[PRIMITIVES.md](./spec/PRIMITIVES.md) (component types), [MODIFIERS.md](./spec/MODIFIERS.md)
(properties), and [EVENTS.md](./spec/EVENTS.md) (events). Component types
include `TEXT`, `BUTTON`, `VSTACK`, `HSTACK`, `SPACER`, and more; stack
constraint properties (`SPACING`, `ALIGNMENT`, …) drive native layout, styling
modifiers (`PADDING`, `COLOR`, `BACKGROUND_COLOR`, …) decorate any view, and
`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` use `-1` = FILL, `-2` = HUG_CONTENT.

## Design Tokens

The renderer owns default token values; the application owns overrides.
Tokens are identified by dot-separated paths (`color.primary`, `space.2`) and
referenced via the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type or overridden globally with
`SET_DESIGN_TOKEN`. See [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system).

## POC Goals

See the GitHub issues (#12, #13, #15, #16, #18):

1. **16-byte opcode engine** — done
2. **Core components & modifiers in Rust** (declarative API) — done
3. **Opcode transport layer** (shared memory + network batch + native C-ABI shim) — done
4. **Rust desktop app with GTK4 renderer** (native shared ring) — done
5. **Native Java library set** (hand-written `com.pathland.view` DSL + signals/computed/effects + reusable HTML renderer + state stores) — done
6. **Quarkus SSR + WebSocket demo** (SSR HTML via `pathland-render-html` + live 16-byte opcode deltas) — done

## Versioning

Pathland follows **Semantic Versioning** (Major.Minor.Patch). The wire protocol
version is 1 (see [OPCODE.md](./spec/OPCODE.md)).

## Contributing

Pathland is open to contributors. Please read:

- [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) — how to build, test, and make changes
- [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) — the Contributor Covenant
- [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md) — how to report a vulnerability (do **not** open a public issue)

Issues are grouped into milestones `1 · Hardening & Memory Safety` through
`5 · Packaging & Grant Readiness`, labelled by epic (`hardening`,
`benchmarking`, `tooling`, `a11y-seo`, `packaging`).

## License

Pathland is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0. See the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file for details.

# Pathland

> Declarative UI, written in your backend. No JavaScript.

**Status: proof of concept.** It works end to end and the tests are green, but the
wire format and APIs may change before 1.0.

[![CI](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

## The pitch

You write the **whole UI in your backend language** — Java, C#, Rust, anything.
Pathland renders the first page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then
keeps it alive with tiny binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth,
reactive UI — delivered by the backend team, without npm, bundlers, a build
pipeline, or a separate frontend.

## What it removes

Today's server team pays for a BFF, a client-side state model, a SPA framework, and
a JS build toolchain — all to render UI the server already owns. Pathland removes
that layer: the backend *is* the application. There is no frontend contract to
maintain, no client state model, and no JavaScript to write.

## How it works

```
You declare the UI in your backend
        │
        ▼
The server renders it (HTML) and owns it
        │
        ▼
Only the things that change travel to the client
        │
        ▼
The client applies them to native elements (60FPS)
```

- **You declare the UI** with a SwiftUI-shaped DSL — `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`,
  styling — right next to your business logic.
- **The server renders and owns it.** The first page is plain HTML (instant paint,
  SEO-friendly); the server keeps the authoritative copy of the UI.
- **Only changes travel.** A click, a signal update, a navigation — the server sends
  a few tiny binary bytes describing exactly what changed. An unchanged screen
  sends nothing. The client applies them to real native elements (browser DOM, GTK
  widgets), so the platform does the layout, animation, and accessibility.

## The whole app

Add one dependency and one bean, and you have a working app.

**Spring Boot**

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); }

    @Bean
    PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
}
```

**Quarkus**

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyApp implements PathlandApp {
    public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); }
}
```

`MyHomeView` is just Java views — the same code runs on both:

```java
public final class MyHomeView implements View {

    State<Integer> count = new State<>(0);   // persisted per session, automatically

    @Override
    public View body() {
        return VStack.of(
                Text.of(Signals.computed(() -> "Clicked " + count.get() + " times")),
                Button.of("Click me", () -> count.update(v -> v + 1))
        ).modifier(Padding.of(24));
    }
}
```

That's it — SSR at any path, live updates over `/ws`, per-session state.

## Why it's smooth

Pathland is built for smooth 60FPS UIs:

- **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes.
  Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees.
- **Native elements, not a canvas.** The browser or OS lays out and animates real
  elements — you get platform layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free.
- **A thin client.** The client is a small static file that hydrates the server HTML
  and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost.

## The part you don't write

The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static
resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend.
(There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.)

## Where it runs today

- **Java** — Spring Boot and Quarkus, with SSR + WebSocket demos.
- **Rust** — a native GTK4 desktop renderer.
- **Designed for** mobile, embedded (LVGL), and in-browser WASM — not built yet.

## Try it

```bash
# one-time: build the Java reactor (the HTML renderer is a Rust library embedded in the jar)
cd lib/java && mvn install

# Spring Boot demo
cd lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-demo
mvn -q package && java -jar target/pathland-spring-boot-demo-0.1.0.jar
# → http://localhost:8080

# Quarkus demo (dev mode with hot reload)
cd lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo
mvn quarkus:dev
# → http://localhost:8080
```

## The technical details

This README is the *what*. The *how* — the wire protocol, the DSL contract, the
conformance vectors, and the implementation notes — lives in [`spec/`](./spec/):

- [OPCODE.md](./spec/OPCODE.md) — the binary protocol
- [DSL.md](./spec/DSL.md) — the authoring surface (what you write)
- [PRIMITIVES.md](./spec/PRIMITIVES.md), [MODIFIERS.md](./spec/MODIFIERS.md), [EVENTS.md](./spec/EVENTS.md)
- [CONFORMANCE.md](./spec/CONFORMANCE.md) — golden byte vectors

## Status & license

Proof of concept. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md),
[CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), and [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md).
Licensed under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE).

49: ## The whole app
50: 
51: Add one dependency and one bean, and you have a working app.
52: 
53: **Spring Boot**
54: 
55: ```java
56: @SpringBootApplication
57: public class MyApp {
58:     public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); }
59: 
60:     @Bean
61:     PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
62: }
63: ```
64: 
65: **Quarkus**
66: 
67: ```java
68: @ApplicationScoped
69: public class MyApp implements PathlandApp {
70:     public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); }
71: }
72: ```
73: 
74: `MyHomeView` is just Java views — the same code runs on both:
75: 
76: ```java
77: public final class MyHomeView implements View {
78: 
79:     State<Integer> count = new State<>(0);   // persisted per session, automatically
80: 
81:     @Override
82:     public View body() {
83:         return VStack.of(
84:                 Text.of(Signals.computed(() -> "Clicked " + count.get() + " times")),
85:                 Button.of("Click me", () -> count.update(v -> v + 1))
86:         ).modifier(Padding.of(24));
87:     }
88: }
89: ```
90: 
91: That's it — SSR at any path, live updates over `/ws`, per-session state.
92: 
93: ## Why it's smooth
94: 
95: Pathland is built for smooth 60FPS UIs:
96: 
97: - **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes.
98:   Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees.
99: - **Native elements, not a canvas.** The browser or OS lays out and animates real
100:   elements — you get platform layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free.
101: - **A thin client.** The client is a small static file that hydrates the server HTML
102:   and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost.
103: 
104: ## The part you don't write
105: 
106: The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static
107: resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend.
108: (There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.)
109: 
110: ## Where it runs today
111: 
112: - **Java** — Spring Boot and Quarkus, with SSR + WebSocket demos.
113: - **Rust** — a native GTK4 desktop renderer.
114: - **Designed for** mobile, embedded (LVGL), and in-browser WASM — not built yet.
115: 
116: ## Try it
117: 
118: ```bash
119: # one-time: build the Java reactor (the HTML renderer is a Rust library embedded in the jar)
120: cd lib/java && mvn install
121: 
122: # Spring Boot demo
123: cd lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-demo
124: mvn -q package && java -jar target/pathland-spring-boot-demo-0.1.0.jar
125: # → http://localhost:8080
126: 
127: # Quarkus demo (dev mode with hot reload)
128: cd lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo
129: mvn quarkus:dev
130: # → http://localhost:8080
131: ```
132: 
133: ## The technical details
134: 
135: This README is the *what*. The *how* — the wire protocol, the DSL contract, the
136: conformance vectors, and the implementation notes — lives in [`spec/`](./spec/):
137: 
138: - [OPCODE.md](./spec/OPCODE.md) — the binary protocol
139: - [DSL.md](./spec/DSL.md) — the authoring surface (what you write)
140: - [PRIMITIVES.md](./spec/PRIMITIVES.md), [MODIFIERS.md](./spec/MODIFIERS.md), [EVENTS.md](./spec/EVENTS.md)
141: - [CONFORMANCE.md](./spec/CONFORMANCE.md) — golden byte vectors
142: 
143: ## Status & license
144:

146: [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), and [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md).

### Current block (lines ~110–118)
```
## Where it runs today

- **Java** — Spring Boot and Quarkus, with SSR + WebSocket demos.
- **Rust** — a native GTK4 desktop renderer.
- **Planned** — mobile apps, embedded devices (LVGL), and in-browser WASM.

Because Pathland is a protocol, the plan is to render the same backend description

```

### Proposed replacement
```
## Where it runs today

- **Java** — Spring Boot and Quarkus, with SSR + WebSocket demos.
- **Rust** — a native GTK4 desktop renderer.

## Where it's headed

Pathland is an open protocol, so the goal is to run the same app logic — written once —
on embedded, mobile, desktop, and browser alike. Today the logic lives in your backend
and the UI is served over WebSocket. Tomorrow it can also run on the device itself:

- **In the browser**, the app logic compiles to WASM, writes to a shared buffer, and the
  main thread is left to rendering alone.
- **On embedded devices**, the logic runs on one core while another core renders, with
  the ring buffer carrying the protocol between them.
- **On mobile and desktop**, the same logic drives native renderers.

Wherever it runs, only tiny binary updates travel across the ring buffer and are applied
in place — nothing is re-rendered or serialized, which is what keeps the UI stutter-free,
even on small devices.
```

This captures: write-once, on-device app logic (WASM + shared buffers / main-thread-only rendering in the browser; logic-core vs render-core split via ring buffer on embedded), and the stutter-free rationale — all informal and honest about being a future goal.

Create a plan for the fix

## Diagnosis

The sidebar in `SplitNavDemo.sidebar()`:

```java
VStack.of(Alignment.FILL, 8, ...)              // ALIGNMENT = FILL (3)
    .modifier(FrameMod.of(200f, Alignment.LEADING))  // ALIGNMENT = LEADING (0) — overwrites it
```

- `FrameMod.of(width, alignment)` emits `ALIGNMENT` (`0x0002`) — the **same property** the VStack constructor uses for its child cross-axis alignment.
- `Modified.render` applies outer modifier props *after* the inner view renders ("outermost wins"), so the node ends with `ALIGNMENT=LEADING`.
- The HTML renderer maps ALIGNMENT → `align-items`: LEADING→`flex-start`, so the menu rows never stretch. The GTK renderer maps it the same way (`child_align` → `Align::Start`), so the bug affects both renderers.

Your `Alignment.FILL` on the VStack is being silently overridden by the frame modifier's `LEADING`.

## Plan

1. **Demo fix (one line)** — `SplitNavDemo.java:87`: change `FrameMod.of(200f, Alignment.LEADING)` → `FrameMod.of(200f, Alignment.FILL)`.
   - Node then emits `ALIGNMENT=FILL` → HTML `align-items:stretch`, GTK `Align::Fill` → the three menu-row buttons stretch to full sidebar width on both renderers. The active-row background highlight becomes a full-width bar, as intended.
2. **Rebuild** — `cargo build -p pathland-render-html` (dylib for the jar embed), then `cd lib/java && mvn -q install` (recompiles `pathland-demo-views` and repackages the demo).
3. **Verify**
   - Java tests green via the `mvn install` run.
   - Start the Spring demo, `curl http://localhost:8080/`, and confirm the sidebar stack div now carries `align-items:stretch` (previously `flex-start`).
4. **Commit** on request only (your uncommitted style tweaks in `HomeView.java` / `css.rs` stay untouched).

## Optional follow-up (not doing unless you want)

The underlying footgun: `frame(...alignment:)` writes the same wire property as a stack's child alignment, so a frame modifier always clobbers a stack's alignment. A DSL-level fix (e.g. `FrameMod` skipping `ALIGNMENT` when applied to a stack, or a distinct frame-alignment property in the protocol) would need spec + renderer + test changes — bigger scope. I'd keep this task to the demo fix unless you want the architectural fix.

- **Specs + status**: `spec/DSL.md`, `spec/MODIFIERS.md` document optional alignment; `pathland-view/status.md` updated.

Found it. There are actually **three** problems stacked on top of each other.

## Why it doesn't work

**1. Key identity mismatch (the main bug)**
`EnvironmentKey` is **identity-based** — `EnvironmentValues.get` walks the chain with `node.key == key` (EnvironmentValues.java:45), and `EnvironmentKey` has no `equals` (EnvironmentKey.java:12-16). So:
- `SplitNavDemo` injects with `EnvironmentKey.of("router")` → instance **A**
- `Sidebar` reads with `EnvironmentKey.of("router")` → instance **B**

A ≠ B → lookup never matches → returns `null`. The key must be a single shared instance. The canonical one already exists: **`Navigation.ROUTER`** (Navigation.java:39).

**2. Reading at field-initializer time (fails even with the right key)**
```java
WritableSignal<Router> router = Environment.value(EnvironmentKey.of("router"));
```
The field initializer runs at `new Sidebar()` — inside `SplitNavDemo.body()`. But `.environment(...)` is a modifier **on the HStack**, and its scope is only pushed by `EnvironmentView.render` *while the HStack subtree renders* (EnvironmentView.java:24-33) — which happens **after** `body()` returns. So at construction the scope isn't active → null regardless of key. The read must move **inside `body()`**, which *is* evaluated during render, inside the pushed scope (Emitter.mount → `root.render(env)` → composite `render` → `body()`, Emitter.java:83, View.java:40-51).

**3. Wrong declared type**
The stored value is a `Router`, but the field is `WritableSignal<Router>` — once keys match, the unchecked cast throws `ClassCastException`.

## Fix plan

1. **`SplitNavDemo.java:55`** — use the canonical key:
   ```java
   .environment(Navigation.ROUTER, router)
   ```
2. **`Sidebar.java`** — drop the field; read in `body()`:
   ```java
   @Override
   public View body() {
       Router router = Environment.value(Navigation.ROUTER);
       return VStack.of(Alignment.FILL, 8, /* menuRow(router, ...) … */) ...
   }
   ```
   Remove the now-unused `WritableSignal` import. `menuRow`/`Navigation.isActive` logic unchanged.
3. **Regression test** — add a test (in `RouterTest`, next to `environmentScopingIsHierarchicalAndScoped`) modeling the exact pattern: a composite whose `body()` reads `Environment.value(key)` under a `.environment(key, value)` modifier returns the injected value (proves env-in-env-composite works).
4. **Verify** — `cd lib/java && mvn -q install` (all tests), then a live check on the Spring SSR that the sidebar renders the three rows (no NPE from a null router).

## Note
The existing test at RouterTest.java:464 reads env inside `render(Environment)` — the correct idiom, which confirms the pattern: **read during render (`body()`), never in a constructor/field.**

Alternative if you'd rather not use env injection: pass the router as a constructor arg (`new Sidebar(router)`). But env injection works fine with the fix above.

Want me to implement this?
In swiftui it is allowed to have it as a field. How can I do something similar here?

Good question — that's exactly what SwiftUI's `@Environment` property wrapper is: a **lazy proxy** whose value resolves at access time (inside `body()`), not at construction. Java has no property wrappers, but we can ship the same ergonomics. Let me check what exists and how `menuRow` consumes it.

**Summary**

Reactivity today is fine-grained: a node re-emits `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY` when a signal bound to its text/property changes (`node.textBinding` / `node.propertyBindings`), and structural slots (`NavigationContainer`, `Conditional`) re-render via `Emitter.reconcileSlot` when their selector signal changes. That covers signals that a node *binds to* — but not signals a view *reads* to decide its structure.

**The gap**

A view that reads a signal inside `render()`/`body()` to pick its subtree (control flow: which branch to render, which router, which destination) is not reactive. `body()` is evaluated once at mount and never re-runs, so that read's dependency is never recorded and no structural change is ever emitted.

**Scope: ALL signals, any source**

This applies to every signal, no matter where it comes from:

- environment values (`Environment.value(key)` returns a `Signal<T>`; a bound node updates, but a `body()` read for control flow does not);
- `State` / `StateStore` signals and `PersistentState` values;
- a `Signals.signal` / `Signals.computed` captured directly by the view;
- host-provided signals (`Platform.ACTIVE_PATH`, viewport, theme, etc.).

Any node whose render depends on a signal should emit its structural changes when that signal changes.

**Mechanism (suggested)**

Generalize `Emitter.reconcileSlot`: render a subtree as a *tracked* computation so that when any signal it read during `render()`/`body()` changes, the subtree re-renders and the structural deltas are emitted.

**Constraints (non-negotiable)**

- Preserve fine-grained per-node reactivity elsewhere — an unchanged node still emits **zero** opcodes.
- Renderers stay stateless (Principle 1).
- Steady-state emission stays allocation-free.
- The diff-based emitter contract is unchanged: only actual changes are transmitted.

**Related**

- `Environment.value(key)` returns signals (feat/environment-signals).
- `spec/DSL.md` §4.5, `AGENTS.md` reactive-signals section, `lib/java/pathland-view/status.md`.
EOF

content.text:
Found it — it's a **timing** problem, not a signal/typing problem.

## Why the field is null

```java
private Signal<Router> router = Environment.value(Navigation.ROUTER);   // Sidebar.java:10
```

Field initializers run at **construction** (`new Sidebar()`). Trace the order in `SplitNavDemo.body()` (SplitNavDemo.java:40-51):

1. `SplitNavDemo.body()` runs — only the **`Platform.ACTIVE_PATH`** scope is active (pushed by the host's `root.environment(ACTIVE_PATH, …)` wrapper).
2. Line 49: `new Sidebar()` → the field initializer runs **now**.
3. Line 51: `.environment(Navigation.ROUTER, router)` only *builds* the modifier — the **`ROUTER` scope is not pushed yet**.
4. The `ROUTER` scope is pushed by `EnvironmentView.render` **while the returned HStack subtree renders** (EnvironmentView.java:25-32) — i.e., *after* `body()` has already returned.

So at step 2, `Environment.value(Navigation.ROUTER)` finds no `ROUTER` binding → returns a constant signal `() -> null`. The field then holds that stale null signal; by the time `Sidebar.body()` runs (ROUTER scope active), the field is already fixed.

**Key point:** `Environment.value(key)` *snapshots the current scope's binding at call time* — it does not return a lazy scope-resolver. Changing the return type to `Signal<T>` changed the type, not the timing. Scoping is only active **during render**, so the read must happen during render (`body()`), not at construction. This is exactly the reason `Environment.Ref` existed — and why reading in `body()` works.

## Options

1. **Read in `body()`** (recommended — 1-line move, matches the new model):
   ```java
   @Override public View body() {
       Signal<Router> router = Environment.value(Navigation.ROUTER);  // scope is active here
       ... menuRow(router.get(), "/home", "Home") ...
   }
   ```
   Works because `body()` is invoked from `render(env)`, inside the pushed scope.

2. **Constructor injection** — `new Sidebar(router)` in `SplitNavDemo` (which already has `router`). Plain Java, no env, no timing issue.

3. **Reintroduce a lazy field proxy** (`Environment.ref(key)`) — the *only* way to keep an env-resolved **field**, since it defers resolution to `.get()` (called in `body()`). Tradeoff: brings back the second thing (`value` + `ref`) you just removed. Note it can't be a plain scope-resolving `Signal<T>` — the emitter's binding effects call `.get()` later, outside the scope, so a "dynamic" env signal would break fine-grained reactivity.

My recommendation is **Option 1** (or Option 2 if you prefer a real field). Which do you want — and if it's 3, should the proxy be `Environment.ref(key)` returning a signal (so it fits the "reads are signals" model)?
Why can't the signal be created with an null value when the field is created in sidebar? And then when the router is set, it will be available in the signal.

Good question — and the answer is the crux of the whole design. Let me be precise.

## Why the field is null

`Environment.value(key)` doesn't return a *live channel* the environment writes into — it returns a **snapshot of the current scope's binding at call time**. The environment is a scoped, hierarchical lookup resolved during render; it never holds a reference to your field, so nothing "sets" it.

At `new Sidebar()` (inside `SplitNavDemo.body()`), the `ROUTER` scope isn't pushed yet → there's no binding to snapshot → you get a constant `() -> null`. A signal created with null *can* later be filled — but only if something writes to that exact signal, and the scope has no way to know about it.

## What your idea actually requires

For a **field** to resolve an env value, the thing it holds must be **lazy** — it must defer resolution to `.get()` (called during render, when the scope is active), not snapshot at construction. That's the `@Environment` property-wrapper trick.

So the real change is: make `Environment.value(key)` return a **lazy, scope-resolving `Signal<T>`** instead of a snapshot. Then:
```java
private Signal<Router> router = Environment.value(Navigation.ROUTER); // captures the *resolver*
...
this.router.get();   // in body(): scope active → the router
```

## The catch (why we didn't do this already)

The emitter reads bound signals **outside** render — e.g. a node binding effect calls `node.textBinding.get()` after render, when the scope is back to empty. A naive lazy signal would resolve to `null` there, breaking `Text.of(Environment.value(key))` reactivity. That's exactly why the current `Environment.value` **snapshots** (so the concrete binding signal is captured and stays correct in effects).

To have both, the lazy signal must **capture the binding during render and reuse it afterwards**:
- `.get()` while a scope is active → resolve the nearest binding, remember it, return its value.
- `.get()` outside render (effects) → use the remembered binding.

That needs a small "in render" marker (e.g. a depth counter bumped by `EnvironmentView` / `NavigationContainer` / `reconcileSlot`), plus per-signal captured state. Edge cases to define: a view instance reused across two scopes; a scope that deliberately binds `null` vs. no scope at all (capture-on-found vs. capture-always).

## Options

1. **Read in `body()`** — works today, no machinery (what we have).
2. **Constructor injection** — `new Sidebar(router)`, plain Java, no env.
3. **Reintroduce a lazy proxy** (`Environment.ref(key)`) — field-friendly; it's the one extra thing you removed.
4. **Make `Environment.value(key)` a lazy, capturing signal** (your idea, done safely) — one accessor, fields work, bindings stay reactive; adds an in-render marker + capture state and a couple of semantics to pin down.

So: your instinct is right in principle — the value just has to be *lazy*, not a snapshot. The question is whether you want to pay for #4's machinery (or #3's extra type) to keep the field style, or use #1/#2.

Which way do you want to go? If #4, I'll write up the exact design (in-render marker, capture semantics, edge cases) before implementing.
limitation is fine

Got it — limitation accepted and documented.

## Finalized design (Option 4)

- `Environment.value(key)` → **snapshot when the key is bound** (concrete signal; preserves `Router`'s `instanceof WritableSignal` and node-binding reactivity), **lazy `EnvironmentSignal` when not bound** (field case; captures on `.get()` during render).
- `EnvironmentSignal<T>`: holds the key; `.get()` re-captures from the current scope when the key is bound, else uses the last captured binding (or `null`).
- `EnvironmentValues.contains(key)` + a `toSignal` helper.
- `Sidebar` field: `private final Signal<Router> router = Environment.value(Navigation.ROUTER);`, `body()` uses `this.router.get()`.
- Tests: new field-style lazy test; keep `environmentValueReturnsSignal` and the bound-router mirror test.
- Docs: `spec/DSL.md` §4.5 + `pathland-view/status.md` note lazy/capturing env signals.
- Documented limitation: a field read *only* by the emitter (never in `body()`) won't capture — inline `Text.of(Environment.value(key))` is the supported form.

One open point before I execute: **Q2 — the hybrid.** I recommend snapshot-when-bound + lazy-when-not (it's what keeps `Router` working unchanged). The alternative is a fully uniform wrapper, which would require changing how `Router` obtains write access.

content.text: Tell me about The alternative- a fully uniform wrapper
Would the uniform be the better design?

Honest answer: **no — for this codebase the hybrid is the better design.** Uniform has real conceptual appeal, but its advantages don't outweigh what it costs here. Here's the reasoning.

## The two designs differ in exactly one place

The lazy wrapper class is **identical** in both. The only difference is what `Environment.value(key)` returns when the key **is** bound:

- **Hybrid:** the concrete binding (the injected `WritableSignal`, or a constant for a plain value).
- **Uniform:** the wrapper anyway (pre-captured).

So "uniform" isn't a different mechanism — it's the choice to route bound reads through a proxy *even when the real signal is right there*.

## Why that makes the hybrid better

1. **Uniform discards information for no gain.** When bound, the hybrid hands back the actual signal — same identity, same `WritableSignal` capability, direct reactivity. Uniform replaces that with a proxy that does the same `.get()` but *loses* identity and capability. You pay complexity and lose fidelity; behavior is otherwise identical.

2. **It forces a Router redesign (reopens Q2).** Because a proxy can't conditionally be a `WritableSignal`, uniform breaks `activePath instanceof WritableSignal` → either you add `Environment.writable(...)` (the accessor you rejected) or a delegating-writable wrapper plus a separate writability check. The hybrid preserves the `Router` exactly as you settled it.

3. **"Always ambient" isn't strictly better — it's differently surprising.** Uniform re-resolves the current scope on every `.get()`. That's closer to SwiftUI during render, but reads that happen *outside* render (the emitter's binding effects) fall back to the last capture anyway — so it's only "ambient" half the time, which is its own asymmetry.

4. **The contract is already uniform where it matters.** Both return `Signal<T>` meaning "the scoped value." The only observable difference is identity/capability — and on that axis the hybrid is strictly *more* capable.

The single genuine merit of uniform — one always-a-proxy rule — is a purity win, not a functional one. And its cost (Router write-access rework, identity changes, no concrete binding) is concrete.

## When uniform *would* be better

If we later want every env read to be a stable, re-resolving handle (e.g., a signal whose value tracks scope changes across re-renders without re-reading), uniform becomes the right call — and at that point the `WritableSignal` capability should become an explicit contract (e.g., a `WritableEnvironmentBinding` interface the `Router` checks) rather than `instanceof`. That's a coherent future direction, but it's a bigger change than what you asked for.

## Recommendation

Go with the **hybrid** now: it preserves every current semantic (node bindings, `Router` mirroring, identity), adds the field style you want, and is the smallest, least surprising change. If you want, I can note the uniform wrapper as a possible future refactor in the issue/status docs.

Shall I proceed with the hybrid as planned?
hybrid

- **`RouterTest`** — new `environmentValueFieldResolvesLazilyAtRenderTime`: a field read before the scope resolves at render; a fresh render under a different binding re-captures; no binding → null.
- **Docs** — `spec/DSL.md` §4.5 + `pathland-view/status.md` document the lazy field style (and the `@Environment`-style example).

- `mvn install`: **81 pathland-view + 15 demo-views tests, 0 failures** (RouterTest 28).
- Live Spring SSR: the sidebar renders all three menu rows via the lazy field.

content.text:
Fixed. The tap now works.

## Root cause
Two bugs in the DOM client (`lib/typescript/src/index.ts`):
1. `POINTER_UP` was only sent for elements matching `<button>` — but the server fires a tap action on `POINTER_UP`, so a gesture on a non-button node never fired. (GTK was unaffected.)
2. Events were attributed to the deepest `[data-pathland-id]` regardless of who listens — clicking the `Text` inside your `VStack` row targeted the `Text` span (no listeners), never the row that declared the gesture.

## Changes

## Objective

## Important Details
- **Environment model (final, hybrid)**: `Environment.value(key)` returns `Signal<T>` — concrete binding (same instance; preserves identity, `instanceof WritableSignal`, reactivity) when the key is bound in the current scope; lazy `EnvironmentSignal<T>` when not yet bound (e.g. field initializer), capturing the binding on the first `.get()` during render and reusing the captured binding outside render.
- `EnvironmentValues.contains(key)` added (distinguishes explicit null binding from absent). `View.environment` has `(key, T)` and `(key, Signal<T>)` overloads; `EnvironmentMod.of(key, Object)`.
- **No `Environment.writable` accessor** (user rejected it — writes stay via the `.environment(...)` modifier). `Router.build(Signal<String>)` / `Router(RouteTable, Signal<String>)`; mirrors navigation back only when the signal is a `WritableSignal` (`instanceof`, hidden inside Router — host `ACTIVE_PATH` always is).
- `Platform.ACTIVE_PATH` is now `EnvironmentKey<String>` (was `EnvironmentKey<WritableSignal<String>>`); `PathlandNode.activePath` is `Signal<String>`.
- **Accepted limitation**: a lazy field whose `.get()` is only called by the emitter (never in `body()`) won't capture — inline `Text.of(Environment.value(key))` is the supported form.

content.text:
You're right that it doesn't use the generic keyed environment — but it's not a fully separate system. There are **two mechanisms inside the same `Environment` class**:

1. **`buttonStyle` — a dedicated, hardcoded slot.** `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE` is its own `ThreadLocal<ButtonStyle>` (`Environment.java:28`), pushed/restored around the subtree by `ButtonStyleView.render` (`ButtonStyleView.java:23-33`), and read by `Button.render` via `env.buttonStyle()` (`Button.java:37`, `Environment.java:41`). It's **not keyed** (`EnvironmentKey`), **not reactive** (returns a raw `ButtonStyle`, not a `Signal`), and not part of `EnvironmentValues`.

2. **The generic keyed scope.** `Environment.VALUES` (`EnvironmentValues`, `Environment.java:29`) is pushed by `EnvironmentView.render` (`EnvironmentView.java:24-32`) and read via `Environment.value(key)` → `Signal<T>`. `EnvironmentView`'s own javadoc calls itself *"the ButtonStyle pattern, generalized"* (`EnvironmentView.java:8`).

So both use the same *technique* — a `ThreadLocal` scoped over the synchronous, single-threaded render pass (`Environment.java:12-14`) — which is why `buttonStyle` reads through `env`. But `buttonStyle` predates the keyed system and never migrated onto it. (Other `*Mod`s like `ControlSizeMod`/`FontWeightMod` aren't inheritance at all — they set a per-node property via `Modified.props`.)

**Concrete consequence of the split:** `Emitter.reconcileSlot` re-applies the keyed scope (`slot.environmentForChildren`, `Emitter.java:345-349`) but **not** `BUTTON_STYLE`. So a structurally re-rendered slot (e.g. a router destination) sitting under a `.buttonStyle(...)` loses the inherited style → its buttons fall back to `PlainButtonStyle`. The keyed scope was explicitly built for that slot case; `buttonStyle` has that gap.

If you'd like, I can plan a migration: make `ButtonStyle` an `EnvironmentKey<ButtonStyle>` (with `PlainButtonStyle` as the default), have `View.buttonStyle(...)` delegate to `.environment(...)`, and read it via `Environment.value(...)`. That would unify it, make it reactive, and fix the slot-rerender gap — at the cost of `Button.render` handling the default fallback. Want me to draft that plan?
Yes. Create a new branch for this. No modifiers should use other inheritance systems than environment. It is the only inheritance system we should have. And update the DSL with this detail.

704: ### 5.6 Custom modifiers (developer-authored)
705: 
706: In SwiftUI any developer can define a modifier that applies to **any** existing
707: view — and Pathland is the same. This is a **first-class, MUST** property of
708: every conformant DSL: modifiers are never hard-bound to a view type.
709: 
710: - **Applicable to any view.** A modifier works on a library primitive
711:   (`Text`), a container (`VStack`), a control (`Button`), a custom view, or an
712:   already-modified view. The same modifier value applies everywhere.
713: - **One mechanism.** Core and application-authored modifiers are the **same
714:   surface**: a `ViewModifier` value applied via `.modifier(...)`. The library's
715:   sugar names (`.padding`, `.foregroundStyle`, …) are conveniences that
716:   construct the built-in `ViewModifier` values; there is exactly one modifier
717:   mechanism ([§5](#5-modifier-surface)). The Java realization ships **no sugar**
718:   — `.modifier(Padding.of(16))` is the only form (plus the `.modifiers(...)`
719:   varargs convenience for several at once).

751: ## 6. Authoring conventions
752: 
753: A conformant DSL follows these conventions:
754: 
755: 1. **Names**: SwiftUI view/modifier names; per-language case (camelCase,
756:    snake_case). `foregroundStyle` not `foregroundColor`; `fontWeight`,
757:    `multilineTextAlignment`, `scaledToFit`, `allowsHitTesting` keep their
758:    SwiftUI spellings.
759: 2. **Signature order**: canonical parameter order is preserved —
760:    `.border(color, width)`, `.frame(width, height, alignment)`,
761:    `.shadow(color, radius, x, y)`. Compound modifiers expand to one property
762:    per argument.
763: 3. **Constructor vs modifier**: structural (alignment, spacing) in the
764:    constructor; everything else chainable.
765: 4. **Typed enums**: `Alignment` (leading/center/trailing/fill),
766:    `TextAlignment`, `FontWeight` (100–900), `Truncation` (head/middle/tail),
767:    `TextCase` (none/uppercase/lowercase), `FontStyle` (normal/italic),
768:    `FontDesign` (default/serif/rounded/monospaced), `ContentMode` (fit/fill),
769:    `ControlSize` (small/regular/large), `ToggleStyle`
770:    (switch/checkbox/button), `PickerStyle` (menu/segmented/wheel/radiogroup),
771:    `DatePickerMode` (date/time/dateAndTime), `ShapeKind`
772:    (circle/rectangle/roundedRectangle/capsule/ellipse/path). Numeric codes
773:    come from MODIFIERS.md's appendix; the DSL resolves them.
774: 5. **`Spacer`/`Color` as views**: `Spacer()` is a flexible expanding filler;
775:    `Color(...)` in a tree is a layout-greedy fill.
776: 6. **Environment scoping**: styles and state that must reach a whole subtree
777:    (`ButtonStyle`, the session's persisted state) are injected via the
778:    environment (Java: thread-local), never threaded through constructors.
779: 7. **Reactivity discipline**: `body()` is evaluated once; a signal read during
780:    mount records a dependency; a later write re-emits only the bound node.
781:    Never mutate signals during mount. The only structural re-evaluation is a
782:    structural container ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-conditional-rendering)),
783:    which the emitter reconciles into `TREE` deltas.
784: 8. **Emission contract**: each DSL call emits exactly the documented
785:    properties with the documented value types; the emitter diffs. The DSL never
786:    computes layout, never positions, never serializes full trees.
787:

790: ## 7. Theme management
791: 
792: Pathland theming is **application-owned over a renderer-owned token system**
793: ([TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md); the wire encoding lives in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md)
794: §Design Token System). The DSL gives the author two distinct surfaces:
795: 
796: 1. **Token references in style modifiers** — semantic intent instead of a
797:    literal: `.foregroundStyle(Color.token("color.primary"))` emits a
798:    `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference the renderer resolves against the current scheme.
799:    No opcode is re-emitted when a token or the scheme changes.
800: 2. **Global theme overrides** — a batch of `STYLE::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands
801:    rolled at mount: a single-scheme `Theme` or an `AdaptiveTheme` light+dark
802:    pair (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**).

358: ### 4.5 Navigation
359: 
360: Navigation is **structural reactivity over a route signal**
361: ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-conditional-rendering)): a
362: `NavigationContainer` is a structural container whose content function is
363: route-table matching. The wire surface is minimal and entirely optional:
364: `ROUTE` (MODIFIERS.md `0x2019`, a STRING current-path property on the slot),
365: `NAV_DEPTH` (MODIFIERS.md `0x201A`, a U32 back-stack-depth property on the
366: slot), `NAV_CHROME` (MODIFIERS.md `0x201B`, an F32-enum chrome-mode property
367: on the slot), `TRANSITION` (MODIFIERS.md `0x1031`, a presentation hint), and
368: the `NAVIGATE` event (EVENTS.md `0x0E`, host→guest). Renderers stay
369: stateless: they render whatever destination subtree the app emits and **may**
370: animate a swap when the `TRANSITION` hint is present, but must render normally
371: when they ignore it.
372: 
373: **Navigation is opt-in — the developer declares it by inserting a
374: `NavigationContainer`.** A tree without one has no navigation and the renderer
375: adds none. The container's chrome mode decides who supplies the navigation UI:
376: 
377: - `PlatformDefault` (default): the **renderer** supplies the chrome — the
378:   platform's native navigation container where one exists (GTK
379:   `AdwNavigationView`, SwiftUI `NavigationStack`, Compose `NavHost`), and a
380:   renderer-drawn back affordance where none exists (the DOM renderer shows a
381:   back button once `NAV_DEPTH > 1`; a no-JS SSR page falls back to the browser
382:   back button). `NavigationContainer.of(router)`.
383: - `Custom`: the **developer owns all navigation UI** — they draw their own
384:   back buttons / bars in the destinations and call `router.back()` /
385:   `navigate(...)` directly; the renderer adds no chrome (no native header-bar
386:   back button, no DOM back button). `NavigationContainer.of(router, Chrome.CUSTOM)`.
387:   Renderers treat a missing `NAV_CHROME` as `PlatformDefault`.
388: 
389: | View | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL (current) | Rust DSL (current) | Emits / Binds |
390: |------|----------------------------|--------------------|--------------------|---------------|
391: | `NavigationContainer` | `NavigationStack(path:) { destination(for:) }` | `NavigationContainer.of(Router)` / `.of(Router, Chrome.CUSTOM)` | `NavigationContainer::new(Router)` | a `Group` slot + `ROUTE` `0x2019`, `NAV_DEPTH` `0x201A`, `NAV_CHROME` `0x201B`, `TRANSITION` `0x1031`; destination swap = `TREE` deltas |
392: | `NavigationLink` | `NavigationLink("label", value:)` | `NavigationLink.of(String, Router, String to)` / `NavigationLink.of(String, String to)` (router-agnostic) | `navigation_link(...)` | a `BUTTON` whose tap pushes `to` (via the router, or resolved to the nearest enclosing router when router-agnostic) |
393: | `RouteTable` | — | `RouteTable` (builder), or `Navigation.navigator(...)` (the ergonomic facade) | `RouteTable::new(...)` | none (app-side matching) |
394: 
395: **Router state** — app-owned (never renderer state):
396: 
397: - `Route` = absolute path + path params (`/users/:id` → `{id:"42"}`) + query.
398:   Path params are strings; typed params are a DSL concern.
399: - `RouteTable` maps path patterns to destination factories, captures params,
400:   and runs **guards**; a guard redirects via `replace()`. Factories are lazy —

Done. Branch `feat/environment-only`, commit `aef4ca6`.

## What changed
- **`Environment.BUTTON_STYLE` is now an `EnvironmentKey<ButtonStyle>`** (`Environment.java:31`); `ButtonStyleMod` binds it via `content.environment(...)`; `Button` reads it through `Environment.value`. The hardcoded `ThreadLocal<ButtonStyle>` slot and `ButtonStyleView` are gone.
- This fixes a real bug: a style scoped above a structural container now survives a destination swap, because `reconcileSlot` re-applies `environmentForChildren`, which captures the keyed scope. (Previously the slot-thread-local wasn't captured → re-rendered destinations fell back to `PlainButtonStyle`.)

## Verification (all other mechanisms audited)
- **Java**: only remaining `ThreadLocal`s are `Environment.VALUES` (the scope's own implementation) and `ReactiveContext.STACK` (signal tracking — not inheritance). `ToggleStyle`/`PickerStyle` are constructor props, not inheritance. **Rust**: no inheritance mechanism exists. 
- **Tests**: 2 new — `buttonStyleIsAKeyedEnvironmentValue`, `buttonStyleScopedAboveAStructuralSlotSurvivesReRender`. `pathland-view` 83, `demo-views` 15, full Java reactor `install` green. (First frame-based assertion was wrong — identical style props are diffed away; the test now asserts the style read at render time, which is the actual regression.)

## Docs
- **`spec/DSL.md`**: §5.5 table (keyed, nearest-wins), new §4.5 bullet, §5.6 Java delta, and §6 item 6 now codify: *the environment is the only inheritance mechanism — a subtree-scoping modifier MUST be an `EnvironmentKey` binding; thread-local is only the implementation of the scope, never a parallel system.*

1: # Pathland
2: 
3: > An open UI protocol — declarative UI, written in your backend. No JavaScript.
4: 
5: **Status: proof of concept.** It works end to end and the tests are green, but the
6: wire format and APIs may change before 1.0.
7: 
8: [![CI](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
9: 
10: ## The pitch
11: 
12: You write the **whole UI in your backend language** — Java, C#, Rust, anything.
13: Pathland renders the first page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then
14: keeps it alive with tiny binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth,
15: reactive UI — delivered by the backend team, without npm, bundlers, an extra build
16: pipeline, or a separate frontend.
17: 
18: ## Pathland is a protocol
19: 
20: The server-rendered path above is the **flagship way to use Pathland today** — not
21: the whole of it. Underneath, Pathland is a **binary UI protocol**: your view
22: declaration compiles to tiny fixed-size opcodes that any renderer can apply to
23: native elements.
24: 
25: That makes it **language- and renderer-agnostic** — a view written in Java, C#, or
26: Rust produces the same opcode stream, and any renderer (browser DOM, native GTK,
27: and on-device ones to come) can apply it. The protocol already drives a **native
28: GTK4 desktop renderer**, and the goal is for your UI code to also run on the
29: device itself — compiled to WASM in the browser, on a dedicated core of an embedded
30: chip, or on native mobile and desktop. Because your views are protocol-defined,
31: they can move to those surfaces later without a rewrite.
32: 
33: Start with the SSR path below and keep it simple — the rest of the protocol is
34: there when you need it (see [Where it's headed](#where-its-headed)).
35: 
36: ## What it removes
37: 
38: Today's server team pays for a BFF, a client-side state model, a SPA framework, and
39: a JS build toolchain — all to render UI the server already owns. Pathland removes
40: that layer: the backend *is* the application. There is no frontend contract to
41: maintain, no client state model, and no JavaScript to write.
42: 
43: ## How it works
44: 
45: ```
46: You declare the UI in your backend
47:         │
48:         ▼
49: The server renders it (HTML) and owns it
50:         │
51:         ▼
52: Only the things that change travel to the client
53:         │
54:         ▼
55: The client applies them to native elements (60FPS)
56: ```
57: 
58: - **You declare the UI** with a SwiftUI-shaped DSL — `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`,
59:   styling — right next to your business logic.
60: - **The server renders and owns it.** The first page is plain HTML (instant paint,
61:   SEO-friendly); the server keeps the authoritative copy of the UI.
62: - **Only changes travel.** A click, a signal update, a navigation — the server sends
63:   a few tiny binary bytes describing exactly what changed. An unchanged screen
64:   sends nothing. The client applies them to real native elements (browser DOM, GTK
65:   widgets), so the platform does the layout, animation, and accessibility.
66: 
67: ## The whole app
68: 
69: Add one dependency and one bean, and you have a working app.
70: 
71: **Spring Boot**

74: @SpringBootApplication
75: public class MyApp {
76:     public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); }
77: 
78:     @Bean
79:     PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
80: }
81: ```
82: 
83: **Quarkus**
84: 
85: ```java
86: @ApplicationScoped
87: public class MyApp implements PathlandApp {
88:     public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); }
89: }
90: ```
91: 
92: `MyHomeView` is just Java views — the same code runs on both:
93: 
94: ```java
95: public final class MyHomeView implements View {
96: 
97:     State<Integer> count = new State<>(0);   // persisted per session, automatically
98: 
99:     @Override
100:     public View body() {
101:         return VStack.of(
102:                 Text.of(Signals.computed(() -> "Clicked " + count.get() + " times")),
103:                 Button.of("Click me", () -> count.update(v -> v + 1))
104:         ).modifier(Padding.of(24));
105:     }
106: }
107: ```
108: 
109: That's it — SSR at any path, live updates over `/ws`, per-session state.
110: *(Imports omitted: `com.pathland.server.PathlandApp`, `com.pathland.view.*`.)*
111: 
112: ## Why it's smooth
113: 
114: Pathland is built for smooth 60FPS UIs:
115: 
116: - **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes.
117:   Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees.
118: - **Native elements, not a canvas.** The browser or OS lays out and animates real
119:   elements — you get platform layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free.
120: - **A thin client.** The client is a small static file that hydrates the server HTML
121:   and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost.
122: 
123: ## The part you don't write
124: 
125: The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static
126: resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend.
127: (There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.)
128: 
129: ## Where it runs today
130: 
131: - **Java** — Spring Boot and Quarkus, with SSR + WebSocket demos (the flagship, getting-started path), and the same shared demo views under the native GTK4 desktop renderer (`pathland-gtk-demo`).
132: - **Rust** — a native GTK4 desktop renderer (same protocol, a second surface).
133: 
134: ## Where it's headed
135: 
136: The SSR path above is the on-ramp — the protocol isn't limited to it.
137: 
138: Write the app logic once, run it on embedded, mobile, desktop, and browser. Pathland
139: is an open protocol, so the same code that drives the server-rendered UI today can
140: also run on the device itself:
141: 
142: - **In the browser**, the app logic compiles to WASM, writes to a shared buffer, and the
143:   main thread is left to rendering alone.
144: - **On embedded devices**, the logic runs on one core while another core renders, with
145:   the ring buffer carrying the protocol between them.
146: - **On mobile and desktop**, the same logic drives native renderers.
147: 
148: Wherever it runs, only tiny binary updates travel across the ring buffer and are applied
149: in place — nothing is re-rendered or serialized, which is what keeps the UI stutter-free,
150: even on small devices.
151: 
152: ## Try it
153: 
154: Each demo has a one-command launcher in [`scripts/`](./scripts/). Run one from the
155: repository root — it builds its own prerequisites (Rust dylibs, the Java reactor)
156: and launches:
157: 
158: | Script | Demo | What you get |
159: |--------|------|--------------|
160: | `./scripts/run-spring-demo.sh` | Spring Boot SSR + WebSocket | http://localhost:8080 |
161: | `./scripts/run-quarkus-demo.sh` | Quarkus SSR + WebSocket (hot reload) | http://localhost:8080 |
162: | `./scripts/run-rust-gtk-demo.sh` | Rust DSL → GTK4 desktop renderer | a native window |
163: | `./scripts/run-java-gtk-demo.sh` | Java DSL → GTK4 desktop renderer (the shared `SplitNavDemo`) | a native window |
164: 
165: ```bash
166: # e.g. the Spring Boot demo
167: ./scripts/run-spring-demo.sh
168: ```
169: 
170: Notes:
171: - The web demos need a JDK 17+ (the whole stack runs on every LTS from 17).
172: - The GTK demos need the GTK4 + libadwaita system libraries.
173: - On macOS the Java GTK demo hands GTK the main thread automatically
174:   (`-XstartOnFirstThread`); Linux needs nothing special.
175: 
176: The same commands without the scripts:
177: 
178: ```bash
179: # one-time: build the Rust HTML renderer (embedded in the jar), then the Java reactor
180: cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-render-html
181: cd lib/java && mvn install
182: 
183: # Spring Boot demo
184: cd lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-demo
185: mvn -q package && java -jar target/pathland-spring-boot-demo-0.1.0.jar
186: # → http://localhost:8080
187: 
188: # Quarkus demo (dev mode with hot reload)
189: cd lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo
190: mvn quarkus:dev
191: # → http://localhost:8080
192: 
193: # Same protocol, native GTK desktop renderer (no browser)
194: cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-render-gtk-demo
195: 
196: # Same protocol via Java: the shared demo views (SplitNavDemo) under the GTK renderer
197: cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi -p pathland-render-gtk
198: cd lib/java/pathland-gtk-demo
199: MAVEN_OPTS="-XstartOnFirstThread" mvn -q compile exec:java \
200:   -Dpathland.core.lib=$PWD/../../lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_core.dylib \
201:   -Dpathland.gtk.lib=$PWD/../../lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_gtk.dylib
202: # (macOS needs -XstartOnFirstThread; Linux can drop it)
203: ```
204: 
205: ## The technical details
206: 
207: This README is the *what*. The *how* — the wire protocol, the DSL contract, the
208: conformance vectors, and the implementation notes — lives in [`spec/`](./spec/):
209: 
210: - [OPCODE.md](./spec/OPCODE.md) — the binary protocol
211: - [DSL.md](./spec/DSL.md) — the authoring surface (what you write)
212: - [PRIMITIVES.md](./spec/PRIMITIVES.md), [MODIFIERS.md](./spec/MODIFIERS.md), [EVENTS.md](./spec/EVENTS.md)
213: - [CONFORMANCE.md](./spec/CONFORMANCE.md) — golden byte vectors
214: 
215: ## Status & license
216: 
217: Proof of concept. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md),
218: [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), and [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md).
