# Customizing your organization's profile

You can share information about your organization by customizing your organization's profile.

## About your organization's profile page

You can customize your organization's Overview page to show a README and pinned repositories dedicated to public users or members of the organization.

Members of your organization who are signed into GitHub, can select a `member` or `public` view of the README and pinned repositories when they visit your organization's profile page.

![Screenshot of an organization's profile page. In the right sidebar, a dropdown menu, labeled "View as: Public", is outlined in dark orange.](/assets/images/help/organizations/profile-view-switcher-public.png)

The view defaults to `member` if either a members-only README or members-only pinned repositories are present, and `public` otherwise.

Users who are not members of your organization will be shown a `public` view.

### Pinned repositories

You can give users easy access to important or frequently used repositories, by choosing up to six repositories for public users and six repositories for members of the organization. Once you pin repositories to your organization profile, the "Pinned" section is shown above the "Repositories" section of the profile page.

Only organization owners can pin repositories. For more information, see [Pinning repositories to your organization's profile](#pinning-repositories-to-your-organizations-profile).

### Organization profile READMEs

You can share information about how to engage with your organization by creating an organization profile README for both public users and members of the organization. GitHub shows your organization profile README in the "Overview" tab of your organization.

You can choose what information to include in your organization profile README. Here are some examples of information that may be helpful.

* An "About" section that describes your organization
* Guidance for getting help in the organization

You can format text and include emoji, images, and GIFs in your organization profile README by using GitHub Flavored Markdown. For more information, see [Getting started with writing and formatting on GitHub](/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github).

## Adding a public organization profile README

> \[!NOTE] Public organization profiles are not available with Enterprise Managed Users.

The content of public `README.md` will appear on your organization's public profile.

1. If your organization does not already have a public `.github` repository, create a public `.github` repository.
2. In your organization's `.github` repository, create a `README.md` file in the `profile` folder.
3. Commit the changes to the `README.md` file.

## Adding a member-only organization profile README

> \[!NOTE] Member-only organization profile READMEs will only load from a `.github-private` repository with its visibility set to private. Repositories in enterprises set to internal visibility will not work.

The content of a member-only `README.md` will be displayed in the member view of your organization's profile.

1. If your organization does not already have a `.github-private` repository, create a private repository called `.github-private`.
2. In your organization's `.github-private` repository, create a `README.md` file in the `profile` folder.
3. Commit the changes to the `README.md` file.

## Pinning repositories to your organization's profile

You can pin repositories that you want to feature, such as those that are frequently used, to your organization's profile page. To choose which repositories to pin to your organization's profile, you must be an organization owner.

1. Navigate to your organization's profile page.

2. In the right sidebar of the page, select the **<svg version="1.1" width="16" height="16" viewBox="0 0 16 16" class="octicon octicon-eye" aria-label="eye" role="img"><path d="M8 2c1.981 0 3.671.992 4.933 2.078 1.27 1.091 2.187 2.345 2.637 3.023a1.62 1.62 0 0 1 0 1.798c-.45.678-1.367 1.932-2.637 3.023C11.67 13.008 9.981 14 8 14c-1.981 0-3.671-.992-4.933-2.078C1.797 10.83.88 9.576.43 8.898a1.62 1.62 0 0 1 0-1.798c.45-.677 1.367-1.931 2.637-3.022C4.33 2.992 6.019 2 8 2ZM1.679 7.932a.12.12 0 0 0 0 .136c.411.622 1.241 1.75 2.366 2.717C5.176 11.758 6.527 12.5 8 12.5c1.473 0 2.825-.742 3.955-1.715 1.124-.967 1.954-2.096 2.366-2.717a.12.12 0 0 0 0-.136c-.412-.621-1.242-1.75-2.366-2.717C10.824 4.242 9.473 3.5 8 3.5c-1.473 0-2.825.742-3.955 1.715-1.124.967-1.954 2.096-2.366 2.717ZM8 10a2 2 0 1 1-.001-3.999A2 2 0 0 1 8 10Z"></path></svg> View as** dropdown menu, then click **Public** or **Member**.

   ![Screenshot of an organization's profile page. In the left sidebar, a dropdown menu, labeled "View as: public" is outlined in dark orange.](/assets/images/help/organizations/org-profile-view.png)

3. Navigate to the settings for pinned repositories.

   * If you already have pinned repositories, in the "Pinned" section, click **Customize pins**.

   ![Screenshot of an organization's profile page. In the top-right corner of the "Pinned" section, "Customize pins" is outlined in dark orange.](/assets/images/help/organizations/customize-pins-link.png)

   * If you haven't yet pinned any repositories, in the right sidebar, click **pin repositories**.

   ![Screenshot of an organization's profile page. In the right sidebar, a link, labeled "pin repositories," is outlined in dark orange.](/assets/images/help/organizations/pin-repositories-org-link.png)

4. In the "Edit pinned repositories" dialog box, select a combination of up to six public, or private repositories to display.

5. Click **Save pins**.

## Changing your organization's profile picture

When you create an organization, GitHub provides you with a randomly generated "identicon." The identicon is generated from a hash of your organization's user ID, so there's no way to control its color or pattern.

You can replace the identicon with an image that represents your organization. To replace the image, you can upload a new image or use a Gravatar image.

1. Here's the README for you to copy-paste. Save it as **`profile/README.md`** in the `PathlandDev/.github` repo (create the `profile` folder first), commit to `main`, and it appears on the org page. GitHub renders the whole file; no comment tricks needed.

````markdown
# PathlandDev

> An open UI protocol — declarative UI, written in your backend. No JavaScript.

[![CI](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

**Status: proof of concept.** It works end to end and the tests are green, but the
wire format and APIs may change before 1.0.

We're building **Pathland**: a protocol-first, cross-language UI protocol. You
write the **whole UI in your backend language** — Java, Rust, anything — and
Pathland renders the first page as server-side HTML (instant, SEO-friendly), then
keeps it alive with tiny binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth,
reactive UI delivered by the backend team — no npm, no bundlers, no separate
frontend.

## What we build

- **A binary UI protocol** — view declarations compile to fixed 16-byte opcodes
  any renderer can apply, so the wire is language- and renderer-agnostic.
- **SwiftUI-shaped DSLs** — `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`, styling — written on the
  backend, right next to your business logic.
- **Native renderers** — the browser DOM (SSR + live WebSocket deltas) today,
  plus a native GTK4 desktop renderer. WASM in the browser, embedded chips, and
  mobile/desktop are the roadmap.
- **Only changes travel** — an unchanged screen transmits zero bytes; updates are
  tiny binary deltas applied in place.

## Repositories

| Repository | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| [Pathland](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland) | The protocol spec, Rust core, Java DSL + Spring/Quarkus starters, renderers, and demos |

More surface is on the way — embedded, WASM, mobile, and desktop targets all speak
the same protocol.

## Try it

Each demo has a one-command launcher in [`Pathland/scripts/`](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/tree/main/scripts):

| Demo | Command |
|------|---------|
| Spring Boot SSR + WebSocket | `./scripts/run-spring-demo.sh` |
| Quarkus SSR + WebSocket (hot reload) | `./scripts/run-quarkus-demo.sh` |
| Rust DSL → GTK4 desktop renderer | `./scripts/run-rust-gtk-demo.sh` |
| Java DSL → GTK4 desktop renderer | `./scripts/run-java-gtk-demo.sh` |

## Get involved

- [Contributing](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) ·
  [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) ·
  [Security](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
- Browse the [protocol spec](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/tree/main/spec) —
  `OPCODE.md` is the wire format, `DSL.md` the authoring surface.
- Licensed under [Apache-2.0](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/blob/main/LICENSE).
````

241: Semantic properties controlling whether and how an element responds to input,
242: plus accessibility. These are the "semantic" (`0x2000`) properties.
243: 
244: | SwiftUI modifier | Protocol property | Type | Emission |
245: | ------------------ | ------------------- | ------ | ---------- |
246: | `.hidden()` | `VISIBLE` 0x100E | U8 (0 = hidden) | one |
247: | `.disabled(_:)` | `ENABLED` 0x2003 | U8 (1 = enabled) | one |
248: | `.allowsHitTesting(_:)` | `ALLOWS_HIT_TESTING` 0x102F | U8 (0/1) | one |
249: | `.controlSize(_:)` | `CONTROL_SIZE` 0x200C | ENUM (`Small`=0, `Regular`=1, `Large`=2) | one |
250: | `.focusable(_:)` | — (via `FOCUS` listener) | — | none (declares `EVENT_LISTENERS` bit 5) |
251: | `.accessibilityLabel(_:)` | `LABEL` 0x200A | STRING | one (arenaRef) |
252: | `.accessibilityRole(_:)` | `ROLE` 0x2001 | ENUM | one |
253: | `.accessibilityState(_:)` | `STATE` 0x2002 | ENUM | one |
254: 
255: ### Semantics
256: 
257: - **`VISIBLE`**: 0 hides the element entirely (removed from layout and hit
258:   testing by the renderer); 1 shows it. Diff-based emission means toggling
259:   visibility emits a single `SET_PROPERTY`.
260: - **`ENABLED`** is the inverse of SwiftUI `.disabled()`: 1 = interactive, 0 =
261:   disabled. Disabled controls do not emit events.
262: - **`.focusable`** has no property: the app requests focus events via the
263:   `FOCUS` listener bit (`EVENT_LISTENERS`, bit 5) and observes
264:   `EVENT::FOCUS_CHANGED` — see [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md).
265: - **`ROLE`/`STATE`** are accessibility enums; their enumerated values are
266:   defined in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md#semantic-properties), not here. `STATE` is
267:   a semantic accessibility property — it never describes visual styling.
268: - **`LABEL`** is a `STRING` property (the accessibility label), distinct from a
269:   `TEXT_FIELD`'s caption label.
270: 
271: ---

272: ### 4.1 Primitive drawing & visual nodes
273: 
274: | View | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) | Java DSL (current) | Emits / Binds |
275: |------|---------------------------|--------------------|---------------|
276: | `Text` | `Text("…")` / `Text(Signal<String>)` | `Text.of(String)` / `Text.of(Signal<String>)` | `TEXT` 0x01; content `SET_TEXT` |
277: | `Image` | `Image("name")` / `Image(systemName:)` | `Image.of()` / `Image.of(String source)` | `IMAGE` 0x02; `IMAGE_SOURCE` 0x1002 |
278: | `Color` | `Color(.sRGB, red:green:blue:)` (a View) | `Color.rgb(int,int,int)` (implements `View`) | `COLOR` 0x03; `COLOR` 0x100A |
279: | `Shape` | `Rectangle()`, `Circle()`, `Capsule()`, `RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius:)` | `Rectangle.of()` | `SHAPE` 0x04; `SHAPE_KIND` 0x0006 |
280: | `Divider` | `Divider()` | `Divider.of()` | `DIVIDER` 0x05 |
281: | `Spacer` | `Spacer()` | `Spacer.of()` | `SPACER` 0x06 |
282: | `ProgressView` | `ProgressView(value:)` / `ProgressView()` | `ProgressView.of(float)` / `ProgressView.of()` | `PROGRESS_VIEW` 0x07; `PROGRESS` 0x200E / `IS_INDETERMINATE` 0x200F |
283: | `Gauge` | `Gauge(value:in:)` | `Gauge.of(float value, float min, float max)` | `GAUGE` 0x08; `VALUE`/`MIN_VALUE`/`MAX_VALUE` |
284: 
285: **Deltas (Java)**: primitives are constructed with `<ViewName>.of(...)`
286: factories (`Text.of("…")`). Full `ShapeKind` coverage ships as named views
287: (`Rectangle.of()`, `Circle.of()`, `Capsule.of()`, `Ellipse.of()`,
288: `RoundedRectangle.of(cornerRadius:)`) plus generic `Shape.of(ShapeKind)` for
289: `Path`.

294: |------|---------------------------|--------------------|---------------|

Here's my plan for the `Label` view.

## Context (from research)
- **The protocol already defines `Label` as a composite** — `spec/PRIMITIVES.md` "Composite views (not primitives)": `Label = HStack + IMAGE + TEXT`, **no component ID, no wire change**. So this is a pure DSL addition.
- This matches your Angular impl (composes `HStack`/`Image`/`Text`) and the "environment-only inheritance" rule we just established: `labelStyle` will be a keyed `EnvironmentKey`, exactly like `buttonStyle`.
- Building blocks exist: `HStack.of(Alignment, float, View...)`, `Text.of(String)`, `Image.of(String)`, `LineLimit.of(int)`, `AccessibilityLabel.of(String)` (→ `LABEL` 0x200A), `Alignment.CENTER`.

## New files (`com.pathland.view`)
1. **`Label.java`** — a composite view via `body()`, mirroring your Angular semantics:
   - `Label.of(String title)` / `Label.of(String title, String icon)`.
   - `body()` reads the scoped style (`Environment.value(Environment.LABEL_STYLE).get()`, default `TitleAndIcon`), then returns:
     `HStack.of(Alignment.CENTER, 2f, …children)` where children are conditionally:
     - icon (if `icon` non-blank **and** style is `IconOnly`/`TitleAndIcon`) → `Image.of(icon)` (no a11y role — the container carries the meaning),
     - title (if `title` non-blank **and** style is `TitleOnly`/`TitleAndIcon`) → `Text.of(title).modifier(LineLimit.of(1))`.
   - Always (when `title` non-blank): `.modifier(AccessibilityLabel.of(title))` on the HStack → the a11y label is the title even in `iconOnly` mode, matching your Angular `aria-label` on the host.
   - Both blank → an empty `HStack.of()` (harmless, consistent with Angular).

2. **`LabelStyle.java`** — enum `TitleAndIcon` (default), `TitleOnly`, `IconOnly`. **DSL-only** (no `wire()`): it's app-side control flow deciding which children to emit — never a wire property, consistent with "only changes matter" (matches your `@if`/`@else` client-side choice, moved to the DSL).

3. **`LabelStyleMod.java`** — `ViewModifier` whose `body(content)` returns `content.environment(Environment.LABEL_STYLE, style)` — environment-scoped, nearest-wins, survives structural slot re-renders (like `ButtonStyleMod`).

## Edits
4. **`Environment.java`** — add `public static final EnvironmentKey<LabelStyle> LABEL_STYLE = EnvironmentKey.of("labelStyle");` + a `labelStyle()` accessor defaulting to `TitleAndIcon` (mirroring `BUTTON_STYLE`/`buttonStyle()`).

## Tests (`LabelTest.java`, `pathland-view`)
- Default (no scope): HStack emits `SPACING=2`, `ALIGNMENT=CENTER`, `LABEL=title`; children = `IMAGE` + `TEXT`; title text has `LINE_LIMIT=1`.
- `titleOnly` → only `TEXT`; `iconOnly` → only `IMAGE`, `LABEL` still = title.
- Blank title/icon suppressed; blank title → no `LABEL` property.
- `labelStyle` env-scoping: `Environment.value(LABEL_STYLE)` read; inner override wins; default when unset; survives a structural slot re-render.

## Docs
- `spec/DSL.md` §4.1: add `Label` row (Java factories, emits `HSTACK`+`IMAGE`+`TEXT`); §5 modifier table: add `labelStyle` row (env-scoped `Environment.LABEL_STYLE`, DSL-only, no property).
- `lib/java/pathland-view/status.md`: add `Label` + `labelStyle`.

## Open questions
1. **Reactive overloads?** Add `Label.of(Signal<String> title, Signal<String> icon)` in v1, or keep static strings only (recommended — mirrors the Angular `input`s and keeps `Text.of(Signal)`/a11y binding wiring out of scope)?
2. **Icon sizing** — leave natural size (recommended; apps can `.frame(...)`), or apply a fixed frame like the Angular's 1em×1em?
3. **Demo usage** — wire a `Label` into the demo (e.g. a sidebar row) to showcase it, or library+tests only?

Everything checks out: `ReactiveValues.from` passes `String` through, and `emitProperty` → `sink.setProperty` encodes STRING props via the arena — so reactive `LABEL` and `IMAGE_SOURCE` bindings work through the existing `propertyBindings` mechanism (same path as `Background.of(Signal)`).

Here's the finalized plan.

## Files

### New — `com.pathland.view` (`lib/java/pathland-view`)
- **`Label.java`** — composite via `body()`:
  - Factories: `of(String title)`, `of(String title, String icon)`, `of(Signal<String> title)`, `of(Signal<String> title, Signal<String> icon)`.
  - `body()` reads `Environment.value(Environment.LABEL_STYLE).get()` (null → `TITLE_AND_ICON`), resolves current title/icon (static or signal `.get()`), and returns `HStack.of(Alignment.CENTER, 2f, children)` where children are conditionally:
    - icon (non-blank **and** style shows icon) → `Image.of(icon)` / `Image.of(iconSignal)` — **natural size**, no a11y role;
    - title (non-blank **and** style shows title) → `Text.of(title)` / `Text.of(titleSignal)` with `.modifier(LineLimit.of(1))`;
  - when title non-blank: `.modifier(AccessibilityLabel.of(title)` / `.of(titleSignal))` on the HStack → a11y label is the title even in `ICON_ONLY` mode (your `aria-label` behavior).
  - Structural presence (add/remove Text/Image) is decided at mount/structural re-render; the *values* stay fine-grained via the signal bindings. (Reactive re-shaping is issue #88 territory — documented.)
- **`LabelStyle.java`** — enum `TITLE_AND_ICON` (default), `TITLE_ONLY`, `ICON_ONLY` + `showsTitle()`/`showsIcon()`. DSL-only: app-side control flow, **never a wire property**.
- **`LabelStyleMod.java`** — `ViewModifier`; `body(content)` → `content.environment(Environment.LABEL_STYLE, style)` (environment-only inheritance, like `ButtonStyleMod`).
- **`LabelTest.java`** — cases: default title+icon (HSTACK with `SPACING=2`, `ALIGNMENT=CENTER`, `LABEL`; `IMAGE`+`TEXT` with `LINE_LIMIT=1`); `TITLE_ONLY` drops icon; `ICON_ONLY` drops text but keeps `LABEL`; blank title/icon suppressed; keyed env read + nearest-wins + default; reactive title re-emits `SET_TEXT`+`LABEL`; reactive icon re-emits `IMAGE_SOURCE`; style survives a structural slot re-render.

### Edit — `com.pathland.view`
- **`Environment.java`** — `public static final EnvironmentKey<LabelStyle> LABEL_STYLE = EnvironmentKey.of("labelStyle")` + `labelStyle()` accessor defaulting to `TITLE_AND_ICON` (parity with `BUTTON_STYLE`/`buttonStyle()`).
- **`Image.java`** — add `of(Signal<String>)`: sets `IMAGE_SOURCE` initial value + `propertyBindings`.
- **`AccessibilityLabel.java`** — add `of(Signal<String>)` → `Modified.prop(Properties.LABEL, signal)` (mirrors `Background.of(Signal)`).

### Demo (`lib/java/pathland-demo-views`)
- New `kitchensink/LabelSection.java` — shows default, `TITLE_ONLY`, `ICON_ONLY`, and a reactive label; wire into `KitchenSinkView`. Icon sources are illustrative strings (renderer-resolved).
- `KitchenSinkViewTest` — add a small assertion (e.g. label title `SET_TEXT` present); existing `>=`/component checks are unaffected.

### Docs

- `spec/PRIMITIVES.md`: already catalogs `Label` as a composite — no change.

content.text:
Done. `Label` is implemented on `feat/label-view`.

## New (5 files)
- **`Label.java`** — composite via `body()`: `HStack(center, spacing 2)` of an optional `Image` + optional `Text` (title gets `LINE_LIMIT=1`); title always becomes the a11y label (`LABEL`), even in `ICON_ONLY`. Factories: `of(title)`, `of(title, icon)`, and all signal/mixed overloads (`Signal<String>` title/icon, static+signal mixes). Blank title/icon suppressed.
- **`LabelStyle.java`** — `TITLE_AND_ICON`/`TITLE_ONLY`/`ICON_ONLY` with `showsTitle()`/`showsIcon()`. DSL-only — never a wire property (the emitted child tree *is* the surface).
- **`LabelStyleMod.java`** — scopes via `content.environment(Environment.LABEL_STYLE, style)` — environment-only inheritance, like `ButtonStyleMod`.
- **`LabelTest.java`** — 8 tests: default (HSTACK `SPACING=2`, `ALIGNMENT=CENTER`, `LABEL`; `IMAGE`+`TEXT`), title-only, icon-only (a11y label kept), blank suppression, keyed env read + default, reactive title (SET_TEXT + LABEL deltas), reactive icon (`IMAGE_SOURCE`), and style surviving a structural slot re-render.
- **`LabelSection.java`** (demo kitchensink) — default/title-only/icon-only labels + a reactive label with a toggle button.

## Edited
- **`Environment.java`** — `LABEL_STYLE` key + `labelStyle()` accessor (default `TITLE_AND_ICON`).
- **`Image.java`** — `of(Signal<String>)` (reactive `IMAGE_SOURCE`); **`AccessibilityLabel.java`** — `of(Signal<String>)` (reactive `LABEL`).
- **`spec/DSL.md`** (§4.1 composite row + note, §5.5 `labelStyle` row) and **`pathland-view/status.md`**.

## Verification
Full reactor `mvn install` green: **121 tests, 0 failures** (view+demo = 106, incl. 8 new Label tests; `KitchenSinkViewTest` now also asserts `IMAGE` + label texts).

One test detail worth noting: reactive nodes with multiple bindings emit one delta *frame per binding*, and `FrameOpcodeSink` only keeps the last — so the reactive tests use a small `AccumulatingSink` in the test file. Nothing committed; say the word if you want a commit.

## Summary

General-purpose accessibility for any node — not just controls — across the DSL, the opcode protocol, and every renderer. Surfaced by the new `Label` view (a composite `HSTACK` + `IMAGE` + `TEXT`, title always driving the accessibility label via `AccessibilityLabel` → `LABEL` 0x200A).

Today the semantic surface is thin: `LABEL` (0x200A), `ROLE` (0x2001), `STATE` (0x2002). It is **not** mapped to ARIA generically, and there is **no** "decorative / hidden from assistive tech" concept at all.

## The gaps

1. **`LABEL` is not a general `aria-label`.** The Rust HTML renderer only reads `LABEL` as a `TEXT_FIELD` caption (`pathland-render-html/src/lib.rs`, the `TEXT_FIELD` arm). A node carrying `AccessibilityLabel` (e.g. every sidebar `Label` row) emits the property on the wire but gets **no** `aria-label`/`role` in the DOM. The Angular reference `Label` sets `aria-label` on the host element.

2. **No `aria-hidden` / decorative support.** An icon-only `Label` (or any purely decorative image) should be hidden from assistive tech while the container's label announces it. There is no protocol property for this; the closest is `ROLE=Image`, which is not the same thing. The Angular reference marks the label's icon `decorative` (a11y-hidden).

3. **`ROLE`/`STATE` → ARIA mapping is incomplete.** Renderers do not yet map the semantic `ROLE`/`STATE` enums (OPCODE.md) onto ARIA roles/states for arbitrary nodes.

## Proposed surface (discussion welcome)

- **Protocol** (`spec/OPCODE.md` + `MODIFIERS.md`): add an `ARIA_HIDDEN` (or `ACCESSIBILITY_HIDDEN`) U8 property (0/1) so any node can be marked decorative/AT-hidden; confirm `LABEL`'s contract is "the accessibility label of any element" (it already reads that way); add golden conformance vectors.
- **DSL** (`com.pathland.view`): add an `AccessibilityHidden` modifier (`ARIA_HIDDEN`); have `Label` mark its icon image hidden in `ICON_ONLY`/`TITLE_AND_ICON` modes (title always drives the a11y label); keep `AccessibilityLabel`/`AccessibilityRole`/`AccessibilityState`.
- **Renderers**: map `LABEL` → `aria-label` (and the element's ARIA role) for **any** node in the Rust HTML renderer + the DOM client; map `ARIA_HIDDEN` → `aria-hidden`; map `ROLE`/`STATE` → ARIA roles/states; mirror the a11y mapping in the GTK renderer (ATK/`GtkAccessible`).
- **A11y semantics**: an element with a `LABEL` should be announced as one accessible element; decorative children (the label's icon) must not double-announce.

## Success criteria

- A node with `AccessibilityLabel` renders `aria-label` in the SSR HTML and DOM deltas (golden vectors updated).
- A decorative icon (`AccessibilityHidden`) renders `aria-hidden="true"` and is not announced.
- Icon-only and title-and-icon `Label`s announce exactly once, with the title.
- `ROLE`/`STATE` produce the correct ARIA role/state in the DOM (and GTK ATK where supported).

## Related

- Issue #65 (WCAG 2.1 AA implementation in the Rust renderer — ARIA + inline styles) is the conformance effort; this issue is the generic protocol + DSL + cross-renderer surface it builds on.
- The `Label` view that surfaced this: branch `feat/label-view` (PR to follow).

1: # Pathland
2: 
3: > An open UI protocol — declarative UI, written in your backend. No JavaScript.
4: 
5: **Status: proof of concept.** It works end to end and the tests are green, but the
6: wire format and APIs may change before 1.0.
7: 
8: [![CI](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
9: 
10: ## The pitch
11: 
12: You write the **whole UI in your backend language** — Java, C#, Rust, anything.
13: Pathland renders the first page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then
14: keeps it alive with tiny binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth,
15: reactive UI — delivered by the backend team, without npm, bundlers, an extra build
16: pipeline, or a separate frontend.
17: 
18: ## Pathland is a protocol
19: 
20: The server-rendered path above is the **flagship way to use Pathland today** — not
21: the whole of it. Underneath, Pathland is a **binary UI protocol**: your view
22: declaration compiles to tiny fixed-size opcodes that any renderer can apply to
23: native elements.
24: 
25: That makes it **language- and renderer-agnostic** — a view written in Java, C#, or
26: Rust produces the same opcode stream, and any renderer (browser DOM, native GTK,
27: and on-device ones to come) can apply it. The protocol already drives a **native
28: GTK4 desktop renderer**, and the goal is for your UI code to also run on the
29: device itself — compiled to WASM in the browser, on a dedicated core of an embedded
30: chip, or on native mobile and desktop. Because your views are protocol-defined,
31: they can move to those surfaces later without a rewrite.
32: 
33: Start with the SSR path below and keep it simple — the rest of the protocol is
34: there when you need it (see [Where it's headed](#where-its-headed)).
35: 
36: ## What it removes
37: 
38: Today's server team pays for a BFF, a client-side state model, a SPA framework, and
39: a JS build toolchain — all to render UI the server already owns. Pathland removes
40: that layer: the backend *is* the application. There is no frontend contract to
41: maintain, no client state model, and no JavaScript to write.
42: 
43: ## How it works
44: 
45: ```
46: You declare the UI in your backend
47:         │
48:         ▼
49: The server renders it (HTML) and owns it
50:         │
51:         ▼
52: Only the things that change travel to the client
53:         │
54:         ▼
55: The client applies them to native elements (60FPS)
56: ```
57: 
58: - **You declare the UI** with a SwiftUI-shaped DSL — `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`,
59:   styling — right next to your business logic.
60: - **The server renders and owns it.** The first page is plain HTML (instant paint,
61:   SEO-friendly); the server keeps the authoritative copy of the UI.
62: - **Only changes travel.** A click, a signal update, a navigation — the server sends
63:   a few tiny binary bytes describing exactly what changed. An unchanged screen
64:   sends nothing. The client applies them to real native elements (browser DOM, GTK
65:   widgets), so the platform does the layout, animation, and accessibility.
66: 
67: ## The whole app
68: 
69: Add one dependency and one bean, and you have a working app.
70: 
71: **Spring Boot**
72: 
73: ```java
74: @SpringBootApplication
75: public class MyApp {
76:     public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); }
77: 
78:     @Bean
79:     PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
80: }
81: ```
82: 
83: **Quarkus**
84: 
85: ```java
86: @ApplicationScoped
87: public class MyApp implements PathlandApp {
88:     public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); }
89: }
90: ```
91: 
92: `MyHomeView` is just Java views — the same code runs on both:
93: 
94: ```java
95: public final class MyHomeView implements View {
96: 
97:     State<Integer> count = new State<>(0);   // persisted per session, automatically
98: 
99:     @Override
100:     public View body() {
101:         return VStack.of(
102:                 Text.of(Signals.computed(() -> "Clicked " + count.get() + " times")),
103:                 Button.of("Click me", () -> count.update(v -> v + 1))
104:         ).modifier(Padding.of(24));
105:     }
106: }
107: ```
108: 
109: That's it — SSR at any path, live updates over `/ws`, per-session state.
110: *(Imports omitted: `com.pathland.server.PathlandApp`, `com.pathland.view.*`.)*
111: 
112: ## Why it's smooth
113: 
114: Pathland is built for smooth 60FPS UIs:
115: 
116: - **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes.
117:   Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees.
118: - **Native elements, not a canvas.** The browser or OS lays out and animates real
119:   elements — you get platform layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free.
120: - **A thin client.** The client is a small static file that hydrates the server HTML
121:   and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost.
122: 
123: ## The part you don't write
124: 
125: The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static
126: resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend.
127: (There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.)
128: 
129: ## Where it runs today
130: 
131: - **Java** — Spring Boot and Quarkus, with SSR + WebSocket demos (the flagship, getting-started path), and the same shared demo views under the native GTK4 desktop renderer (`pathland-gtk-demo`).
132: - **Rust** — a native GTK4 desktop renderer (same protocol, a second surface).
133: 
134: ## Where it's headed
135: 
136: The SSR path above is the on-ramp — the protocol isn't limited to it.
137: 
138: Write the app logic once, run it on embedded, mobile, desktop, and browser. Pathland
139: is an open protocol, so the same code that drives the server-rendered UI today can
140: also run on the device itself:
141: 
142: - **In the browser**, the app logic compiles to WASM, writes to a shared buffer, and the
143:   main thread is left to rendering alone.
144: - **On embedded devices**, the logic runs on one core while another core renders, with
145:   the ring buffer carrying the protocol between them.
146: - **On mobile and desktop**, the same logic drives native renderers.
147: 
148: Wherever it runs, only tiny binary updates travel across the ring buffer and are applied
149: in place — nothing is re-rendered or serialized, which is what keeps the UI stutter-free,
150: even on small devices.
151:

153: 
154: Each demo has a one-command launcher in [`scripts/`](./scripts/). Run one from the
155: repository root — it builds its own prerequisites (Rust dylibs, the Java reactor)
156: and launches:

# Pathland

> An open UI protocol. Declarative UI, written in your backend — language- and renderer-agnostic.

**Status: proof of concept.** It works end to end and the tests are green, but the
wire format and APIs may change before 1.0.

[![CI](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/michaelkrog/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

## Pathland is a protocol

Pathland is a **binary UI protocol** — not a framework, and not a single rendering
target. Your view declaration compiles to fixed 16-byte opcodes that any renderer
applies to native elements. The wire is the contract: a view written in Java, Rust,
C#, or anything else produces the **same opcode stream**, and any renderer can
apply it.

That makes Pathland **language- and renderer-agnostic**:

- **Write the UI once**, in your backend language, right next to your business logic.
- **Run it on any surface.** The same view code drives today's server-rendered web
  and the native GTK4 desktop renderer — and is on track for the browser via WASM,
  embedded devices, and native mobile/desktop ([Where it's headed](#where-its-headed)).
- **Only changes travel.** The protocol is a stream of tiny binary deltas: an
  unchanged screen transmits zero bytes, and updates are applied in place.

**Server-side rendering is the first surface we ship** — the flagship
getting-started path — **not the whole story**. It's the on-ramp that's useful
today; the protocol underneath is where the portability comes from.

## The flagship path today: SSR

The fastest way to replace a BFF + JavaScript-frontend stack. You write the **whole
UI in your backend language** — Java, C#, Rust, anything. Pathland renders the first
page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then keeps it alive with tiny
binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth, reactive UI — delivered by
the backend team, without npm, bundlers, an extra build pipeline, or a separate
frontend.

```
You declare the UI in your backend
        │
        ▼
The server renders it (HTML) and owns it
        │
        ▼
Only the things that change travel to the client
        │
        ▼
The client applies them to native elements (60FPS)
```

- **You declare the UI** with a SwiftUI-shaped DSL — `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`,
  styling — right next to your business logic.
- **The server renders and owns it.** The first page is plain HTML (instant paint,
  SEO-friendly); the server keeps the authoritative copy of the UI.
- **Only changes travel.** A click, a signal update, a navigation — the server sends
  a few tiny binary bytes describing exactly what changed. An unchanged screen
  sends nothing. The client applies them to real native elements (browser DOM, GTK
  widgets), so the platform does the layout, animation, and accessibility.

## The whole app

Add one dependency and one bean, and you have a working app.

**Spring Boot**

```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); }

**Quarkus**

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyApp implements PathlandApp {
    public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); }
}
```

`MyHomeView` is just Java views — the same code runs on both:

```java
public final class MyHomeView implements View {

    State<Integer> count = new State<>(0);   // persisted per session, automatically

    @Override
    public View body() {
        return VStack.of(
                Text.of(Signals.computed(() -> "Clicked " + count.get() + " times")),
                Button.of("Click me", () -> count.update(v -> v + 1))
        ).modifier(Padding.of(24));
    }
}
```

That's it — SSR at any path, live updates over `/ws`, per-session state.
*(Imports omitted: `com.pathland.server.PathlandApp`, `com.pathland.view.*`.)*

## What it removes

Today's server team pays for a BFF, a client-side state model, a SPA framework, and
a JS build toolchain — all to render UI the server already owns. Pathland removes
that layer: the backend *is* the application. There is no frontend contract to
maintain, no client state model, and no JavaScript to write — and the same backend
code that serves the web can drive other renderers later.

## Why it's smooth

Pathland is built for smooth 60FPS UIs:

- **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes.
  Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees.
- **Native elements, not a canvas.** The platform lays out and animates real
  elements — you get native layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free,
  whether those elements are DOM nodes or GTK widgets.
- **A thin client.** The web client is a small static file that hydrates the server
  HTML and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost.

## The part you don't write

The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static
resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend.
(There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.)

## Where it runs today

- **Web (SSR + live WebSocket deltas)** — Java, with Spring Boot and Quarkus
  starters and demos; the flagship getting-started path.
- **Native desktop (GTK4)** — a renderer driven by the same protocol, from both the
  Rust DSL and the shared Java demo views (`pathland-gtk-demo`).

Two surfaces, one protocol — the demos' shared views run under both without a
rewrite.

## Where it's headed

The SSR path above is the on-ramp — the protocol isn't limited to it.

Write the app logic once, run it on embedded, mobile, desktop, and browser. Pathland
is an open protocol, so the same code that drives the server-rendered UI today can
also run on the device itself:

- **In the browser**, the app logic compiles to WASM, writes to a shared buffer, and the
  main thread is left to rendering alone.
- **On embedded devices**, the logic runs on one core while another core renders, with
  the ring buffer carrying the protocol between them.
- **On mobile and desktop**, the same logic drives native renderers.

Wherever it runs, only tiny binary updates travel across the ring buffer and are applied
in place — nothing is re-rendered or serialized, which is what keeps the UI stutter-free,
even on small devices.

## Try it

Each demo has a one-command launcher in [`scripts/`](./scripts/). Run one from the
repository root — it builds its own prerequisites (Rust dylibs, the Java reactor)
and launches:

| Script | Demo | What you get |
|--------|------|--------------|
| `./scripts/run-spring-demo.sh` | Spring Boot SSR + WebSocket | http://localhost:8080 |
| `./scripts/run-quarkus-demo.sh` | Quarkus SSR + WebSocket (hot reload) | http://localhost:8080 |
| `./scripts/run-rust-gtk-demo.sh` | Rust DSL → GTK4 desktop renderer | a native window |
| `./scripts/run-java-gtk-demo.sh` | Java DSL → GTK4 desktop renderer (the shared `SplitNavDemo`) | a native window |

```bash
# e.g. the Spring Boot demo
./scripts/run-spring-demo.sh
```

Notes:
- The web demos need a JDK 17+ (the whole stack runs on every LTS from 17).
- The GTK demos need the GTK4 + libadwaita system libraries.
- On macOS the Java GTK demo hands GTK the main thread automatically
  (`-XstartOnFirstThread`); Linux needs nothing special.

The same commands without the scripts:

```bash
# one-time: build the Rust HTML renderer (embedded in the jar), then the Java reactor
cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-render-html
cd lib/java && mvn install

# Spring Boot demo
cd lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-demo
mvn -q package && java -jar target/pathland-spring-boot-demo-0.1.0.jar
# → http://localhost:8080

# Quarkus demo (dev mode with hot reload)
cd lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo
mvn quarkus:dev
# → http://localhost:8080

# Same protocol, native GTK desktop renderer (no browser)
cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-render-gtk-demo

# Same protocol via Java: the shared demo views (SplitNavDemo) under the GTK renderer
cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi -p pathland-render-gtk
cd lib/java/pathland-gtk-demo
MAVEN_OPTS="-XstartOnFirstThread" mvn -q compile exec:java \
  -Dpathland.core.lib=$PWD/../../lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_core.dylib \
  -Dpathland.gtk.lib=$PWD/../../lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_gtk.dylib
# (macOS needs -XstartOnFirstThread; Linux can drop it)
```
